title: 3D Environments with Games Characteristics for Teaching History: The VRLerna Case Study
statistical_results: Mean correct answers rose from 7.57 (pre-test) to 13.43 (post-test). Wilcoxon signed-rank test showed the improvement was statistically significant (Z=-2.226, p=0.026). Motivation results: 64% found the experience very or extremely interesting; 53% found it very or extremely entertaining; 35% reported the environment contributed much or very much to triggering imagination; 47% reported the game created a mysterious atmosphere generating curiosity; 59% considered VRLerna contributed much or very much to understanding the educational content; 64% considered the 3D object rotation feature contributed much or very much to careful observation of archaeological finds.
key_outcomes: Statistically significant improvement in learning performance after using VRLerna. The application succeeded in attracting student interest (64% found it very/extremely interesting) and providing entertainment (53% found it very/extremely entertaining). The majority of students (59%) felt VRLerna contributed to understanding the prehistoric period in Greece.
engagement_results: 64% of students found the experience very or extremely interesting; 53% found it very or extremely entertaining; 35% reported the environment triggered their imagination much or very much (though 48% said 'a little' and 18% said 'not at all'); 47% reported the game created a mysterious atmosphere generating curiosity.
comparative_methodology: Within-subjects pre-post test design without a control group. Students completed a pre-test after a 25-minute lecture, then interacted with VRLerna for 45 minutes, followed by a post-test. The Wilcoxon signed-rank test was used due to the small sample size and concerns about normality.

title: 3D Game-Based Approach to Learning Ancient Malay Heritage's History
statistical_results: Reading session: highest score was 3 out of 10 questions correct; 3 out of 19 completed reading but had difficulty answering. Playtesting session: all 19 participants completed the game; average duration 13 minutes; highest score 9 out of 10 questions correct. Survey results: 71% found it easier to play 3D games and understand the story; 94% agreed 3D games can create interest to learn history; 85% agreed 3D game visualizes ancient Malay heritage better than textbook images; 77% agreed playing game can relate with the history of Hikayat Hang Tuah.
key_outcomes: Students performed substantially better on verbal history questions after playtesting the 3D game (highest 9/10) compared to after reading textbook content (highest 3/10). Students showed more engagement and interest with the game compared to reading. The animation in the game related to history taught in school, interactions enhanced interest, and challenges provided motivation.
engagement_results: Students read textbook content in monotone and were less interested in reading the whole content. In contrast, school children seemed to love playing the 3D game based on their feedback. The interaction in the game enhanced interest in children to keep playing and gaining knowledge. The challenges in the game gave motivation to complete the game.
comparative_methodology: Within-subjects informal comparison: same group of 19 participants completed a reading session (textbook content) and a playtesting session. Performance on verbal quiz compared informally (highest score 3/10 for reading vs 9/10 for game).

title: A case study of the in-class use of a video game for teaching high school history
key_outcomes: Two major themes emerged: (1) Student engagement - students were significantly more active and engaged during game sessions compared to traditional lectures; students discussed game content outside of class; students described the experience as fun, hands-on, and challenging; even self-described non-gamers found the game enjoyable. (2) Teaching strategies and classroom integration - the teacher evolved his implementation over four years, developing strategies including teachable moments, goal orientation/reflection/position taking, and scaffolding for learning to play the game. The classroom shifted from a traditional teacher-centered environment to a learner-centered one where the teacher became a facilitator/guide rather than lecturer. However, the game did not guarantee learning - some students still had incomplete understanding on post-game quizzes.
engagement_results: Strongly positive engagement results across all four class sections. Students were visibly more active and engaged during game play compared to traditional lecture. Specific evidence: students discussed the game outside of class (at lunch, between classes); students described the experience as fun, hands-on, and challenging; one student noted 'no one was asleep because everyone was into the game'; the game extended engagement beyond class boundaries with students seen standing outside the computer lab windows observing gameplay; even non-gamers reported enjoyment.
comparative_methodology: Qualitative comparison between traditional teacher-centered classroom sessions (observed one day before game use) and game-based sessions (observed over three days). No formal experimental control group or statistical comparison.

title: A game for learning history on mobile devices
statistical_results: Descriptive statistics only (frequencies and percentages). No inferential statistical tests reported. Gender differences in game preferences were described but not statistically tested in this paper.
key_outcomes: The study produced a detailed understanding of Portuguese students' mobile game preferences and habits that informed the design of the '1910' history game. Key findings: male students prefer longer, competitive games (GTA, CS, PES, Minecraft) while female students prefer casual games (Pou, Subway Surfers). Students strongly endorsed using games for learning school content (84.6%). Eight of Gee's 36 learning principles were identified in the most popular games and applied to the game design: Psychosocial Moratorium, Committed Learning Principle, Amplification of Input, Achievement Principle, Practice Principle, Regime of Competence, Intuitive Knowledge, and Affinity Group Principle.
engagement_results: Students showed high receptivity to using games in course activities. They valued repetition of tasks for cognitive/motor skill development and identification with game characters. The paper notes students are receptive and like games that allow development of cognitive skills or motor dexterity.

title: A Pilot Evaluation of a Virtual Reality Educational Game for History Learning
statistical_results: Spearman's correlation between reality judgement and other variables: reality judgement correlated significantly with focus (r=.70, p<.001), autotelic experience (r=.69, p<.001), and perceived learning (r=.45, p<.05). Reality judgement correlated significantly with all variables except Hedonic Identity. Individual items: focused on tasks (M=5.82, SD=1.3), experience left feeling great (M=5.64, SD=1.87), prefer to learn history with similar environments (M=5.30, SD=1.83), would learn faster this way (M=5.48, SD=1.89), felt part of virtual world (M=5.96, SD=1.26), felt as active participant of narrated story (M=5.56, SD=1.22).
key_outcomes: Students' general assessment of the VR game was positive across all measured dimensions. They considered the game as simple, innovative, valuable, inspiring, challenging, practical, predictable and appropriate for learning about history. Students reported strong focus during gameplay and high sense of presence in the virtual environment. The correlation analysis revealed that making the learning environment feel more real was crucial for its success, as reality judgement was significantly correlated with focus, autotelic experience, and perceived learning.
engagement_results: Students were focused on tasks during the entire game duration (Focus M=5.71, SD=1.30). They reported high autotelic experience (M=5.82, SD=1.47), feeling great about the experience (M=5.64, SD=1.87). Students felt present in the virtual environment: felt part of the virtual world (M=5.96, SD=1.26), considered themselves active participants in the narrated story (M=5.56, SD=1.22). Focus group discussions confirmed students were excited, impressed with the 3D virtual environment, and felt immersed. Students reported the instructional design managed to hide formal learning processes under the umbrella of the VR game.

title: Acquiring the History of the City with Collaborative Game Based Learning
key_outcomes: Students can acquire home town historical facts through collaborative gameplay, though retention varies significantly by quest type (visual/colour tasks best retained at 70%, date-based tasks worst at 27%). Over 73% of students were positively motivated by the collaborative game-based learning experience. 23 out of 30 students found acquiring historical knowledge through the 3D maze game interesting. Students showed greater willingness to cooperate in groups during gameplay compared to their general learning preferences (54% prefer independent learning normally, but collaborative gaming shifted preference).
engagement_results: Over 73% were positively motivated by the collaborative game-based learning; almost 17% were not motivated; 10% were negatively motivated. 23 out of 30 students said acquiring historical knowledge with the 3D maze game could be interesting. Primary motivations among game players were mental challenge and social experience.

title: An Exploration of Computer Game-Based Instruction in the "World History" Class in Secondary Education: A Comparative Study in China
study_design: quasi-experimental pretest/posttest comparative study with mixed methods (quantitative and qualitative)
statistical_results: Hypothesis 1 (Learning achievement): Pretest means not significantly different (CGBI M=13.53 vs NCGBI M=13.21, t=0.51, p=.61). Posttest CGBI (M=18.22) significantly higher than NCGBI (M=16.92, t=2.01, p=.05). Hypothesis 2 (Motivation): Overall motivation CGBI (M=22.34) significantly higher than NCGBI (M=21.37, t=2.05, p=.04). Availability of learning materials dimension significantly higher in CGBI (M=7.71 vs M=6.83, p=.00). Overall appeal and educational value not significantly different. Hypothesis 3 (Gender achievement): No significant gender differences in learning achievement in either class (CGBI: female M=17.53, male M=18.98, t=-1.48, p=.14; NCGBI: female M=17.45, male M=16.68, t=1.01, p=.31). Hypothesis 4 (Gender motivation): Boys significantly more motivated by CGBI than girls in both Class A (male M=24.15, female M=20.79, t=5.32, p=.04) and Class B (male M=22.85, female M=19.98, t=3.48, p=.002).
key_outcomes: CGBI produced significantly greater learning achievement than NCGBI. Participants were significantly more motivated by CGBI compared with NCGBI, particularly in the availability of learning materials dimension. No significant gender differences in learning achievement were found. Boys were significantly more motivated by CGBI than girls in both classes.
engagement_results: Qualitative data showed strong engagement: male students were familiar with the game, felt excited about using it for education, and valued its role in memorizing historical events. Female students, though less familiar with the game, expressed curiosity and interest when games were applied to education, and nearly universally agreed that games could make education less tedious and improve learning. Both genders eagerly longed for future learning via gaming.
comparative_methodology: Paired samples t-tests for comparing CGBI vs NCGBI on biographic data, pretest/posttest scores, and motivational dimensions. Independent samples t-tests for comparing gender differences in learning achievement and motivation within each class. SPSS used for quantitative analysis. Qualitative data from open-ended questions analyzed through summarizing and reasoning.
game_type: commercial off-the-shelf (COTS) real-time strategy computer game

title: An Investigation of the Influence of Learning Effectiveness and Motivations in a Taiwan History Digital Game – Govern Formosa
statistical_results: Learning effectiveness: pretest M=26.48 (SD=17.640) to posttest M=60.00 (SD=16.350), t=8.196***, p<.001. Motivation: pretest M=23.07 (SD=4.739) to posttest M=27.52 (SD=3.130), t=5.064***, p<.001. System: pretest M=24.41 (SD=3.703) to posttest M=26.81 (SD=4.161), t=3.314*, p=.003. Content: pretest M=24.63 (SD=3.477) to posttest M=27.37 (SD=3.564), t=3.635**, p=.001. Memory: pretest M=43.33 (SD=6.127) to posttest M=49.15 (SD=5.953), t=4.786***, p<.001.
key_outcomes: All measures showed statistically significant improvements from pretest to posttest. Learning effectiveness scores more than doubled. Students' learning motivations significantly improved. The game was found to be feasible and effective for game-based learning in history courses. Students felt satisfied about the game and were willing to continue self-learning after school. A postponed test showed history knowledge memory was retained over time.
engagement_results: Students found the game intriguing and it attracted them to continue self-learning after school. Students were willing to play again. Memory aspect results showed students believed the game helped them memorize history content and connect to questions in assessments.
comparative_methodology: Paired Samples t-test comparing pretest and posttest scores for learning effectiveness and all four questionnaire aspects (motivation, system, content, memory)

title: Application of Virtual Reality and Gamification in the Teaching of Art History
study_design: Single-group post-test only (user elicitation study with questionnaire-based evaluation)
statistical_results: Cronbach's Alpha = 0.753 (acceptable internal consistency). VR Usability: highest mean scores for Application ease of use (4.20) and Realism (4.13); lowest for Organization (3.47). CV for VR usability ranged from 0.099 to 0.192 (good, under 20%). VLE evaluation: highest mean for Easy manipulation (2.27) and Learning (2.13); lowest for Utility (1.67). CV for VLE ranged from 0.12 to 0.43. Strongest correlations in VR usability: Task-Navigation (0.715), Navigation-Movement (0.717). No significant correlations found in VLE evaluation.
key_outcomes: Students achieved good interaction with the application; the VR usability was rated positively with means mostly above 3.5 on a 5-point scale; the application improved learning in Art History and motivated students; strong correlations found between task completion, navigation, and movement in VR usability; no single dominant variable in VLE evaluation
engagement_results: Students reported positive interaction with the virtual museum; motivation in learning scored a mean of 1.87 (on VLE scale); satisfaction scored 2.07; sense of belonging in the virtual environment scored 1.93; intention to use the application scored 1.93. The authors concluded the application achieved 'more active learning'.
game_type: Virtual reality educational game (virtual museum with gamification elements)

title: Are Pairs More Attentive Towards Feedback Than Individuals? A Glance Into Feedback Neglect for Middle-School Students Using an Educational Game in History
study_design: Quasi-experimental within-subjects repeated measures design with two conditions (individual play vs. pair play on a shared tablet)
statistical_results: PlayCnd[Pair]: coefficient = -1.20, OR = 0.30, p < .05. AchLev[MediumLower]: coefficient = -0.79, OR = 0.45, p = 0.07. Nr (trial number): coefficient = -0.38, OR = 0.68, p < .01. TaC[QuiteWrong]: coefficient = -0.89, OR = 0.41, p < .001. TaC[VeryWrong]: coefficient = -1.47, OR = 0.23, p < .001. Interaction AchLev[MediumLower]:PlayCnd[Pair]: coefficient = 1.64, OR = 5.16, p < .01. Nr:PlayCnd[Pair]: coefficient = 0.37, OR = 1.45, p < .05. Three-way interaction Nr:AchLev[MediumLower]:PlayCnd[Pair]: coefficient = -0.45, OR = 0.64, p < .05.
key_outcomes: Medium/lower-achieving students were more attentive towards feedback when working in pairs compared to working individually. Higher-achieving students were more inclined to attend to feedback when playing individually than in pairs. However, higher-achieving students playing in pairs were more resilient to repeated failing, maintaining consistent attention to CCF across multiple trials. The probability of attending to CCF decreased with more errors on a task (Quite Wrong and Very Wrong categories) and with repeated failures on the same task.
engagement_results: Students tended to dismiss CCF to a larger extent after several attempts on the same task. Higher-achieving students playing in pairs were less sensitive to this decline from repeated failing, suggesting collaborative settings may buffer higher-achievers against frustration-driven feedback neglect. A teachable agent was noted to have a stronger impact on feedback acceptance than pair play in comparison to earlier studies.
comparative_methodology: Within-subjects design comparing individual play vs. pair play on the same tablet. Students played in both conditions across two sessions (35-40 min each). Order was counterbalanced (single-to-pair vs. pair-to-single) randomly assigned to each class. Students were matched into homogeneous pairs by achievement level.
game_type: Educational history game (drill-and-practice with narrative elements, concept maps, timelines, multiple-choice questions)

title: "Assassin's Creed reminds us that history is human experience": Students' senses of empathy while playing a narrative video game
study_design: qualitative interview study (semistructured interviews, narrative inquiry, inductive thematic analysis following Creswell's data analysis spiral)
key_outcomes: Students described (1) a sense of immediate access to history contrasting with school-based memorization learning; (2) a sense of human connection to people in the past through both fictional and historical characters; (3) increased perception of multiple perspectives in history (e.g., British Loyalist perspective, Native American perspective during American Revolution); (4) willingness to allow the games to rewrite their beliefs about history and reshape their identities (e.g., revised views of George Washington, the Crusades, slavery, and Catholic Church history); (5) theorizing about historical accuracy with high trust in game designers. However, students tended to miss opportunities for critical engagement, evidencing uncritical trust in Ubisoft's portrayals and risk of presentism.
engagement_results: Students demonstrated high affective engagement with the game. They contrasted positive emotional associations from gameplay with disengagement from memorization-based school history. Students described visceral feelings of being 'put into' history, feeling terror during the Boston Massacre scene, developing empathy for enslaved people through character embodiment, and experiencing emotional connections that prompted identity reflection. 11 of 14 participants reported conducting online searches inspired by the games.
game_type: commercial off-the-shelf (COTS) narrative action-adventure video game

title: Battle Card, Card Game for Teaching the History of the Incas Through Intelligent Techniques
study_design: Design-based research with acceptance testing (pre-test/post-test surveys and interviews with schoolchildren)
statistical_results: Satisfaction survey results: 80% found the game attractive; 60% clearly understood the dynamics of the game; 100% of schoolchildren commented they would play it again. Performance test: game loading time 5.386 seconds. Unit tests: 3 specs, 0 failures.
key_outcomes: The game was evaluated through unit tests (all passed), performance tests (5.386s loading time), and acceptance tests using game quality metrics. Satisfaction surveys with schoolchildren showed positive reception: 80% found it attractive, 60% understood the dynamics, and 100% would play again. The overall results showed educators and specialists could use Battle Cards as a pedagogical tool in student learning.
engagement_results: 80% of schoolchildren found the game attractive; 100% stated they would play it again; students suggested improvements to graphic design and visual effects, indicating engagement with the game

title: Building a virtual Roman city: teaching history through video game design
key_outcomes: Qualitative findings based on student response papers (17/45), course evaluations (22/30 commented on the project), classroom observations, and analysis of the 3D buildings produced. Most groups (9 out of 10) successfully integrated research content into their 3D building designs. All groups were able to use Unity 3D without catastrophic failures. Students showed incremental improvement in technical proficiency over the six-hour design sessions. Course evaluation feedback was overwhelmingly positive: students described the project as 'stimulating', 'interesting', 'fun', 'engaging', and 'creative'. One student called it 'probably the most fun assignment I have done during my time at university'. Multiple students recommended keeping the project as a permanent course component. Only one student found it 'not fleshed out enough to be worthwhile'. Some groups exceeded expectations by creating custom objects and importing external textures beyond the prefabricated asset package.
engagement_results: Strongly positive student engagement. Of the 22 course evaluation comments about the Virtual City Project, nearly all were positive. Students reported high levels of enjoyment, found the combination of technology and history stimulating, and multiple students recommended the project be continued in future iterations. Students reported that the hands-on design process helped them learn more about their assigned structures than traditional methods would have.
game_type: student-designed 3D virtual environment / VR simulation using game engine

title: Changing Students' Perceptions of a History Exploration Game Using Different Scripts
statistical_results: K=5 LCA model selected (AIC=97602, BIC=98181, VLMR=0.048, BLRT<0.01, Entropy=0.861). Script effects: Humor No Snark script -- players more likely in 'Liked It All' vs 'Didn't Like Jo' (OR=1.519); Snark No Humor script -- 'Didn't Like Jo' vs 'Didn't Like History' (OR=1.660), 'Didn't Like Jo' vs 'Liked It All' (OR=1.820), 'Liked It All' vs 'Not Very Funny' (OR=1.506). Reading level effects: strong readers more likely in 'Liked It All' vs 'Didn't Like Any' (OR=2.362), and other comparisons ranging from OR=1.377 to OR=1.715. Benjamini & Hochberg post-hoc correction applied.
key_outcomes: Five distinct player engagement profiles identified: 'Didn't Like Anything' (N=184, 7%), 'Didn't Like Jo' (N=546), 'Didn't Like History' (N=489), 'Liked It All' (N=665, 28%), and 'Not Very Funny' (N=533). Removing humor or snark from the game script shifted some students' engagement profiles. Removing either humor or snark from the base script made players more open to positive evaluations of history learning, though at the cost of worsened attitudes toward the main character Jo. Higher reading level was associated with greater overall game enjoyment across all groups.
engagement_results: Students generally enjoyed the game, with 'Liked It All' being the largest group (28%) and 'Didn't Like Any' the smallest (7%). Script changes primarily affected the malleable middle groups ('Not Very Funny', 'Didn't Like History', 'Didn't Like Jo') rather than extreme groups ('Liked It All' and 'Didn't Like Anything'). The Snark No Humor script produced the most significant shifts in group membership.
comparative_methodology: Four script conditions compared: (1) Initial Design (Snark + Humor), (2) No Snark (Humor only), (3) No Humor (Snark only), (4) No Humor No Snark. Latent class membership proportions compared across conditions using 3-step procedure in MPlus. Reading level included as a covariate.
game_type: Point-and-click history adventure game (digital, narrative-driven exploration game)

title: Code Book©- The development of an Adventure Action Game for History Instruction and the Evaluation of Flow State, Learning Performance and Gender Difference
statistical_results: Paired-samples t-test: pretest M=1.32 (SD=1.25) vs posttest M=2.68 (SD=1.45), t=-5.33, p<0.001. Flow antecedents M=3.63 (SD=0.67); Flow experience M=3.73 (SD=0.59). Gender differences: flow antecedents t=0.12, p=0.906; flow experience t=-0.29, p=0.774; pretest t=1.30, p=0.201; posttest t=0.85, p=0.400 (all non-significant)
key_outcomes: Significant improvement in history knowledge after game-based learning (p<0.001). Learners reached high flow state (all dimension means above median 3.00). No significant gender differences in flow state or learning performance, suggesting the game is suitable for both genders.
engagement_results: High flow state achieved: flow antecedents M=3.63, flow experience M=3.73 (both above median 3.00). Highest flow antecedent sub-dimensions: feedback (M=3.68) and playability (M=3.68). Highest flow experience sub-dimensions: concentration (M=3.80) and time distortion (M=3.79), indicating high learner attention and immersion.
comparative_methodology: Within-subjects comparison (pretest vs posttest); between-subjects comparison by gender (male n=11 vs female n=27)

title: Design of a SmartArt Classroom in Art History: A Learning Experience with Self-Regulated Serious Games
study_design: Design-based research (system design and description, no empirical evaluation with participants)
statistical_results: No original statistical results. Referenced finding: gamified teaching explains 72% of the variance in learning outcomes (from cited meta-analysis by Gallego-Durán et al. 2014).
key_outcomes: This is a design paper presenting the SmartArt virtual classroom. No empirical outcomes from actual implementation are reported. The paper claims, based on literature review, that the combination of serious games with SRL increases motivation, creativity, and deep learning. The design is intended to facilitate self-regulated learning of art history content.
game_type: Serious game / graphic adventure videogame with gamification elements

title: Designing a Role-play Game for Learning Taiwan History and Geography
study_design: design and development research (no empirical evaluation reported)
key_outcomes: No empirical outcomes are reported. The paper is a design and development study only. The authors expect that the game will enhance learning effectiveness and motivation for Taiwan history and geography. Future work is planned to include pre- and post-tests for learning achievement, questionnaires for learning motivation, learning attitudes, and satisfaction, plus focus group interviews.

title: Designing and evaluating a mobile educational game "Void Broken 2.0" for history instruction
statistical_results: Paired-samples t-test: Posttest M=13.62 (SD=5.66) vs. Pretest M=7.88 (SD=4.38), t=9.58, p<.001. Average progress score was 5.74 points (max possible progress = 18). Game evaluation: Overall M=4.29 (SD=0.53); Perceived Usefulness M=4.29 (SD=0.58); Perceived Ease of Use M=4.14 (SD=0.70); Game Elements M=4.41 (SD=0.63). Gender differences (independent-samples t-test): No significant difference in history learning performance (t=-1.98, p=.052); Significant difference in overall game evaluation (t=2.35, p=.022), perceived usefulness (t=2.83, p=.006), and perceived ease of use (t=2.09, p=.041) favoring males; No significant difference in game elements evaluation (t=1.10, p=.276).
key_outcomes: Students' history learning performance improved significantly after playing Void Broken 2.0. All game evaluation dimensions scored above the median (3.0), indicating the game was perceived as useful, easy to use, and satisfying in terms of game elements. Male students perceived the game as more useful and easier to use, but no significant gender differences were found in learning performance or game elements evaluation.
engagement_results: Overall game evaluation mean was 4.29 out of 5.0 (SD=0.53), well above the median of 3.0. Game elements evaluation was highest at M=4.41 (SD=0.63). Students were reported to be very active during gameplay and many wanted to play the full version in the future.
comparative_methodology: Pretest-posttest comparison within a single group using paired-samples t-test; gender comparison using independent-samples t-test.

title: Designing Computer Simulation Game for Learning the History of the Kingdom of Majapahit
study_design: Design-based research (game design and development, first stage only; no empirical evaluation)
education_level: Primary/secondary education (Indonesian curriculum context; game also designed with undergraduate student involvement)
key_outcomes: No empirical evaluation was conducted. The paper presents a design-phase project only. Expected outcomes described conceptually include: increased student interest in Majapahit history, ability to challenge known conceptions through experimentation and observation, emotional engagement with historical narrative, development of analytical thinking through strategy gameplay, and providing students with a different perspective compared to course books.

title: Development of a game for History Course of Secondary School Students
study_design: Qualitative design-based research (classroom observation, preliminary interviews, prototype development, and cognitive walkthrough evaluation with think-aloud technique)
key_outcomes: Qualitative outcomes from cognitive walkthrough with 8 teachers: (1) The game environment start screen was perceived as attractive and engaging; (2) Sound clips and text-to-speech were found very helpful for learning and memorizing content; (3) Variety of practice test question types gained teacher attention and interest; (4) Overall evaluation of game was satisfactory and accepted by teachers; (5) Teachers confirmed the prototype could help engage and motivate students. No quantitative student learning outcome data was collected.
engagement_results: Teachers reported that the game prototype environment was attractive and increased interest to play it. Participants found the pause/stop feature and text-to-speech helpful for understanding content. The practice test variety was appreciated for gaining attention and interest. However, excessive animations were found distracting and hindered focus on content. Teachers confirmed the prototype addresses the identified need for an interactive, non-lecture-based approach to history teaching.
game_type: Digital game-based learning (DGBL) prototype - desktop application

title: Development of Educational Game for Indonesian History Lesson Focusing on Indonesia Pre-Literacy Relics 'Prehistoria' for Grade X High School Student
study_design: Design and development research with post-play survey using 5-point Likert scale questionnaire
statistical_results: Descriptive statistics only (frequency counts and averages). Average play time per level: Level 1 = 38.96s, Level 2 = 63.2s, Level 3 = 60s, Level 4 = 64.1s, Level 5 = 28.1s. Total average game time = 254.36 seconds. 60% recognized puzzle genre, 40% recognized adventure genre. No inferential statistics reported.
key_outcomes: The game was successfully developed and is playable in approximately 4-5 minutes. Many ancient objects were well-recognized by respondents (e.g., Cave Painting by all 5 respondents, Menhir and Planting by 4). However, some objects (Trilobites, Cephalaptis, Ax, Moko) were recognized by only 1 respondent. Age recognition was problematic, with one respondent not recognizing any historical age. The survey identified multiple usability issues including difficult-to-use arrow movement controls, disruptive UI, hard-to-understand health and toggle status features, and a strong need for a tutorial.
engagement_results: Enemy challenge was rated as adequate (3 of 5 respondents rated it 'Good'). Difficulty perception varied widely among respondents. 4 of 5 respondents said a tutorial would benefit the game. UI was perceived as disruptive by 3 of 5 respondents. Arrow movement was perceived as very difficult to use by 3 of 5 respondents.
game_type: Puzzle-adventure digital educational game (2D, WebGL browser-based)

title: Digital Game-based learning (DGBL) model and development methodology for teaching history
study_design: mixed-methods (preliminary needs analysis via questionnaire and interview, document analysis, and literature review leading to model proposal)
explicit_definition: DGBL is a paradigm which utilizes the game as a medium for conveying the learning contents, it is all about leveraging the power of computer games to captivate and engage endusers for a specific purpose, such as to develop new knowledge and skills. DGBL is also defined as an application which uses the characteristics of video and computer games to create engaging and immersive learning experiences for delivering specified learning goals, outcomes and experiences.
statistical_results: Descriptive statistics only (percentages from survey). No inferential statistics. No pre/post intervention comparison as the game was not yet developed.
key_outcomes: The study identifies key problems in history learning (difficulty memorizing facts, lack of interest, boring teaching methods) and demonstrates student readiness for game-based learning. It proposes a DGBL model and DGBL-ID development methodology but does not yet report learning outcomes from an actual game intervention.
engagement_results: Survey findings indicate high student engagement with digital games in general: 92% have played digital/electronic games, 83.6% like to play games. Students prefer racing (67.2%), adventure (62.1%), and fighting games (55.9%). Key requirements for GBL history courseware include illustrating historical facts clearly (70.6%), increasing students' interest (66.7%), and learning history via entertained experience (65.5%).
game_type: digital game-based learning (DGBL) courseware / educational game

title: Educational Computer Game for learning History: Impact on learners' level of knowledge and learners' satisfaction
study_design: Quasi-experimental with pre-test/post-test control group design
education_level: Secondary school (average age 18-20, from different schools in Kairouan)
explicit_definition: Van Eck (2006) defined educational computer games as 'an interactive play that teaches learners how to achieve goals and how some serious problems can be solved' and as 'a game explicitly designed with learning purposes, where the role of fun is obvious and required.' Roger Caillois defined a game as an activity that is fun, separate, uncertain, non-productive, controlled by rules, and fictitious.
statistical_results: Wilcoxon signed-rank test results: Phase 1 (traditional): pre-test avg=5.65, post-test avg=7.85, progression rate=2.2, W=9, p<=0.01. Phase 2 (game): pre-test avg=5.25, post-test avg=8.37, progression rate=3.12, W=0, p<=0.01. Both results significant at p<=0.01. TAM satisfaction results: Usefulness avg=1.62 (median=1), Ease of Use avg=1.95 (median=2), Attitude avg=1.78 (median=1), Behavioral Intention avg=2.62 (median=2).
key_outcomes: Both traditional learning and the educational computer game had a positive impact on learners' level of knowledge (both significant at p<=0.01). The game group showed a slightly higher progression rate (3.12) compared to the traditional group (2.2). Game group post-test average (8.37) was higher than traditional group post-test average (7.85). Learners showed high satisfaction with the game across all TAM dimensions (averages ranging from 1.62 to 2.62 on a 1-7 scale).
engagement_results: High learner satisfaction measured via TAM: Usefulness (avg=1.62, median=1), Ease of Use (avg=1.95, median=2), Attitude toward using (avg=1.78, median=1), Behavioral Intention to use (avg=2.62, median=2). All averages were close to 1 (maximum satisfaction) and far from 7 (maximum dissatisfaction), indicating participants were very satisfied with the educational computer game.
comparative_methodology: Two-group comparison: control group (N=20) used traditional learning (4-page printed course), experimental group (N=16) used the educational computer game. Pre-test evaluated baseline knowledge; post-test evaluated knowledge gain. Wilcoxon signed-rank test used for statistical significance.
game_type: Educational computer game (2D action game, browser-based)

title: Engaging Students in Developing a Stereoscopic 3D Educational History Game
key_outcomes: No formal evaluation was conducted. The authors report observational outcomes: students seemed engaged and motivated to learn; several skills were developed including strategic thinking, decision-making, collaboration, and problem-solving. Spatial thinking was advanced but the extent was not measured.
engagement_results: Students volunteered enthusiastically to participate. The game design process coupled curricular and extracurricular activities. Students-designers evaluated situations, chose actions, judged results, and received feedback.

title: Exploration on the Effectiveness of Learning, Interest, and Attitude of the Integration of Review System of History Based on Mobile Game and Forgetting Curve
study_design: Quasi-experimental (non-equivalent control group design with pre-test and post-test)
statistical_results: Learning achievement: First pretest - Experimental M=61.43 SD=28.202, Control M=64.78 SD=27.858, t=-0.397, p=0.374 (not significant). Second pretest - Experimental M=60.48 SD=23.817, Control M=58.26 SD=28.492, t=0.329, p=0.372 (not significant). Posttest - Experimental M=75.62 SD=17.107, Control M=72.78 SD=16.368, t=0.562, p=0.2885 (not significant). Learning attitude: Pretest p=0.202 (not significant); Posttest - Experimental M=4.95 SD=0.736, Control M=4.46 SD=0.88, t=1.996, p=0.026 (significant). Learning interest: Pretest p=0.54 (not significant); Posttest - Experimental M=4.75 SD=1.092, Control M=4.05 SD=1.081, t=2.12, p=0.02 (significant).
key_outcomes: No statistically significant differences in learning achievement scores between groups across all three tests, though the experimental group's mean scores were higher in the second pretest and posttest. Significant improvement in learning attitude (p=0.026) and learning interest (p=0.02) for the experimental group compared to the control group after the intervention.
engagement_results: The game-based review system significantly improved student learning attitude and interest. Students expressed desire to learn content to advance in the game, enhancing their awareness of goals and initiative. Multimedia features of the game improved learning interest, and students exhibited enthusiasm and devoted time to the course.
comparative_methodology: Quasi-experimental design comparing an experimental group (game-based review system on tablet within 20 minutes after lesson) versus a control group (traditional teacher-led oral review). Both groups received the same history instruction from the same teacher.
game_type: Mobile game-based review system (digital game-based learning on tablet)

title: Fostering Perspective-Taking in History Students Through Board Games
study_design: qualitative case study with interaction analysis and qualitative coding of written artifacts and video data
key_outcomes: Analysis of 71 written commentaries from 29 students showed evidence of all five targeted perspectives in every document. Perspective-taking was demonstrated through classroom interactions and written reflections. Over time (Commentary 1 to Commentary 9), students showed increasing adoption of 'Greek at the Time' and 'Responding to Events' perspectives, while 'City-State' perspective and 'Situated Strategy' references decreased, suggesting internalization of the game world. Strategy: Situated (72 total code counts) and RP: Role (61 total code counts) were the most frequently coded design elements. Students unanimously reported this was one of their favorite history classes ever, with several calling it the best class they had ever taken.
engagement_results: Students unanimously reported high engagement and enjoyment; the course was described as one of their favorite history classes and by some as the best class ever taken. All 71 coded documents showed evidence of at least one of the five perspective types.
comparative_methodology: Informal comparison by the instructor: students developed deeper insights into the intricacies of Greek motivations compared to other classes run by the same professor, but lacked the breadth of knowledge evident in students from lecture-based courses. No formal statistical comparison was conducted.

title: Game Based Learning Model for History Courseware: A Preliminary Analysis
study_design: Mixed methods: document analysis of SPM performance reports (2002-2005), questionnaire survey, and teacher interviews; followed by a design proposal (GBL Model)
education_level: Secondary school (Form Four, equivalent to 10th grade)
explicit_definition: Game Based Learning (GBL) is defined as: (1) a paradigm which utilizes the game as a medium for conveying the learning contents (citing Tan et al.); (2) leveraging the power of computer games to captivate and engage end users for a specific purpose, such as to develop new knowledge and skills (citing Corti); (3) an application which uses the characteristics of video and computer games to create engaging and immersive learning experiences for delivering specified learning goals, outcomes and experiences (citing Freitas).
statistical_results: No inferential statistics reported. Only descriptive percentages from the survey. SPM history failing percentage was 25.6% in 2005 and rose to 34.3% in 2006. STPM history failing percentage was 45.11% in 2005.
key_outcomes: Key findings: (1) History is perceived as boring and difficult due to memorization demands; (2) Students are ready for digital game-based learning as most already play digital games regularly; (3) Main requirements for GBL history courseware are: illustrate history facts clearly (70.6%), increase students' interest (66.7%), and learn history via entertained experience (65.5%); (4) A GBL Model for history courseware design was proposed with pedagogy and digital games as main components.
engagement_results: 83.6% of students like playing digital/electronic games. Students play games primarily for fun (72.9%), to fill free time (62.7%), and enthusiasm with fantasy world (45.2%). Students see advantages of gaming as fun (53.7%), filling free time (50.8%), calming thoughts (49.2%), and increasing creativity (47.5%). Teachers agreed that GBL can help increase students' interest and performance in history and reduce boredom.
game_type: Game-based learning courseware (proposed model, not yet implemented)

title: Game based technology to enhance the learning of history and cultural heritage
key_outcomes: System tested by more than 100 users with diverse backgrounds; received positive feedback. No formal quantitative or qualitative outcome data reported.

title: Game-based augmented reality learning of Sarawak history in enhancing cultural heritage preservation
study_design: Prototype development and evaluation using questionnaire-based usability and functional testing with GameFlow scale analysis
education_level: Not specified (general participants, no restriction on age or job position)
statistical_results: Cronbach's alpha reliability estimates: Flow antecedents = .0286 (low/poor); Challenge = .1428 (poor); Feedback = .4631; Playability = .4456; Flow experiences = .6527 (generally good reliability); Concentration = .5616; Control = .6471 (reasonable); Knowledge = .4590. Mean scores ranged from 3.85 to 4.75 on a 5-point scale.
key_outcomes: Participants felt mediocre about the challenge and knowledge factors of the prototype. The GameFlow scale found that challenge and knowledge factors have low reliability. The design of game challenge is the major factor improving flow experience, but flow antecedents show poor reliability. Knowledge factor has room for improvement and is more relatable to the study objective. The study highlights enhancement of cultural heritage preservation through AR game-based experiences learned from James Brooke's history in Sarawak.
engagement_results: Usability testing measured five factors: Knowledge (items about improving history knowledge, understanding hints, wanting to learn more), Autonomy (understanding game walkthrough, distance indicator use, sense of control), Immersion (not noticing time passing, emotional investment in scores/titles, game absorption), Challenge (hints helping with quizzes, increasing difficulty, suitable difficulty), and Social Interaction (cooperating with teammates, ease of joining, collaboration improving skills). Mean scores generally above 4.0 on a 5-point scale suggest positive engagement.
game_type: Augmented reality game-based learning (location-based, multiplayer, collaborative treasure hunt)

title: Gamification and the History of Art in Secondary Education: A Didactic Intervention
study_design: Longitudinal qualitative study (4 academic years: 2017/2018 to 2020/2021, applied in 1st, 2nd, and 4th year of ESO)
education_level: Secondary education (Compulsory Secondary Education / ESO, ages 12-17)
explicit_definition: The paper quotes a definition from Marin and Hierro (2013): 'Gamification is a technique, a method and a strategy at the same time. It starts from the knowledge of the elements that make games attractive and identifies, within a specific activity, task or message, in a Non-game environment, those aspects that can be converted into a game or ludic dynamics. All this to achieve a special involvement, on the part of the users, encourage a change in their behavior or transmit a message or content. That is to say, create a significant and motivating experience.' (p. 14)
statistical_results: No inferential statistics reported. Results are based on qualitative analysis of 536 textual sources (learning diary entries) across three intervention phases (168 entries in 1st ESO, 230 in 2nd ESO, 138 in 4th ESO) and comparison of average grades. Art History grades progressively increased across academic years while general grades remained stable.
key_outcomes: Positive effect on learning Art History skills with progressive improvement over time. Art History grades consistently higher than general subject grades and increasing across years. Growth in motivation for studying Art History. Progressive development of positive vision about art history (from 11.5% with no references to positive vision to 27.3% with very explicit abundant presence). Generally positive assessment of gamification strategies, though with uneven evaluations across different strategies.
engagement_results: Favorable assessments of gamification strategies by students: Discovery learning (68% favorable in 1st ESO), Narrative gamification (71% in 1st, 65% in 2nd, 81% in 4th ESO), Use of rewards (91% in 1st, 88% in 2nd, 72% in 4th ESO), Break Out (92% in 2nd ESO), Escape Room (66% in 4th ESO), Assessment games (77% in 1st ESO). Students reported high engagement with narrative elements and rewards. Some strategies like Escape Room and Break Out generated mixed feelings including stress and nervousness in some students.
comparative_methodology: Within-subjects longitudinal comparison: (1) comparison of average grades in general Geography and History subject vs. gamified Art History assessment tools across three academic years; (2) longitudinal tracking of same students across four academic years to observe evolution of learning outcomes and attitudes
game_type: Multiple gamification strategies (discovery learning, narrative gamification, challenge-based learning, rewards, escape room, break out, gamified evaluation tools)

title: Gamification, Pandemic and Learning the History of Ideas. Experiments in the Context of Core Curriculum
study_design: Qualitative autoethnographic research (teacher-researcher autoethnography with ethnographic recording of student interventions)
key_outcomes: The study reports qualitative outcomes from autoethnographic field notes across 10 serious games played over 80 sessions. Key findings include: (1) Games developed 'historical consciousness' — the ability to reflect critically on historical time and understand the otherness of past societies. (2) Students developed hermeneutic and intersubjective reasoning by establishing conceptual mediations with historical characters. (3) Games fostered historical imagination — the ability to construct abstract concepts and fictional scenarios from diverse experiences. (4) Students developed a sense of contingency — understanding that philosophical ideas are not universal truths but mental constructions within specific spatiotemporal coordinates. (5) Games promoted contextualization ability — students learned to situate authors' thought in precise spatiotemporal coordinates. (6) The fictional para-identity of gameplay created a 'radical otherness' that allowed students to think beyond their usual values and worldviews. (7) Games served as epistemic rituals breaking pandemic monotony and the productivist time of virtual education. (8) Group identifications formed during games translated into real friendships, overcoming pandemic isolation.
engagement_results: Students became highly engaged with the game activities. In the Juego de los Sueños, after the first session students spontaneously requested a winner be declared and asked for explanations about which team's solution best reflected Descartes' philosophy, showing that victory and quality of reflection mattered equally. Students broke the solipsism of the pandemic through game-based group identification. The games functioned as 'pure events' that disrupted the cadence of quarantines and virtual deliveries, adding narrativity to the courses.
game_type: Serious games (custom-designed tabletop/role-playing games conducted via Zoom)

title: Gamifying History: Designing and Implementing a Game-Based Learning Course Design Framework
study_design: Mixed-methods (pre-/post-questionnaires, two focus groups, and two in-class observations by a third-party research assistant)
explicit_definition: The authors distinguish between gamification and game-based learning: 'gamification referring to the addition of game-based elements—such as points and leaderboards, conflict, or competition (Whitton 2014)—onto an already established learning activity or assessment. Game-based learning, then, is the integration of game-based principles into the design of a learning activity or assessment.' They also define engagement as 'a learner's active participation in not only class and team discussions, but also in one's willingness to go above and beyond in the course, completing additional assignments... or accessing external material that is not being assessed.'
statistical_results: No formal statistical tests were reported. Findings are primarily qualitative with descriptive percentages from questionnaires. 80% of pre-questionnaire students chose the course for the topic/time period interest; 20% for scheduling. Six of 12 participating students completed at least one optional side-quest. By end of semester, all respondents ranked the role-playing game as the most engaging course element.
key_outcomes: Team-based nature and embedded gameplay elements were most effective at improving engagement. The two-week role-playing game was universally ranked as the most engaging part of the course. Students expressed strong interest in historical empathy through role-play. Initial confusion about gamified terminology (assignments, format/schedule, creature names) declined substantially over time. Students who stated they preferred lectures were observed to be consistently engaged during team-based activities. Extrinsic rewards (team prize of a plushie) had limited motivational impact; the team-based competition itself was more motivating. Side-quests had inconclusive engagement results—some students found them motivating while others needed stronger incentivization.
engagement_results: Engagement increased through team-based collaboration and competition, with students reporting a heightened sense of belonging and willingness to exceed expectations. The role-playing game component generated the highest engagement. Students were least engaged during team presentations to other teams. Observations showed students stopped taking detailed notes within 10 minutes but remained consistently engaged during collaborative activities. By end of course, students wished there had been more team-based game activities and expressed desire for more gamified elements.
comparative_methodology: Pre-/post-questionnaire comparison of student perceptions before and after the gamified course. The study compared student stated preferences (e.g., for lectures) with observed in-class behavior (e.g., engagement during team activities). No control group was used.
game_type: Game-based learning course design framework (gamified course structure with embedded role-playing game)

title: Grand Theft Longboat: Using Video Games and Medievalism to Teach Medieval History
key_outcomes: No formal evaluation conducted. The author reports informal observations: 'the majority of students have shown a very good if not excellent understanding of the aim of exercise, displaying high levels of both creativity and effort in their pitches'; 'module feedback from students is consistently very positive in terms of what students feel they have gained both intellectually, and in terms of enjoyment.' Student quote: 'This module represented a very creative way to look at history... The pitch and essay are also a really different way of being assessed and make it a lot more fun.'
engagement_results: Students reported high engagement and enjoyment. The author notes students 'exceeded my expectations in demonstrating the potential of video games as a medium for representing authentic versions of the Middle Ages and enabling engagement with medieval history.' Students exercised 'greater initiative and autonomy' compared to a previous traditional module.

title: History on the Game Board: The Use of Board Games in Polish History Education
study_design: Mixed methods: pre-post anonymous surveys with open-ended questions, in-depth qualitative interviews, and classroom observation/practitioner report
education_level: High school and university (history teacher training)
key_outcomes: Substantial knowledge gains about communist-era Poland after playing Kolejka (from zero knowledge to detailed associations). Strong development of historical empathy (80% could articulate feelings about historical people's experiences). Emotional engagement including frustration, anger, joy, sympathy, and helplessness mirroring historical experiences. Near-universal intent among future teachers to adopt game-based methods (100% of 20 interviewed final-year students). Students reported games made abstract historical periods tangible, helped reconstruct historical atmosphere, and facilitated retention of facts, dates, and causal relationships. Intergenerational bonding through games about People's Poland era.
engagement_results: Students expressed high excitement and satisfaction with game-based learning. Frequent student comments: 'This is how I can learn history', 'This kind of history is not boring.' Students reported emotional responses including frustration, helplessness, anger, and joy during Kolejka gameplay. Post-game interviews revealed students found game-based history 'a great example of historical reconstruction on the board.' For Twilight Struggle, students noted that 'facts, dates, numbers and people formed a coherent story' and they felt they 'went back in time and relived history.' Students autonomously sought additional information via smartphones during games.
comparative_methodology: Pre-post survey design for the Kolejka workshop: students answered identical questions before and after the game session. No control group. The dramatic shift from 0% knowledge pre-game to high percentages post-game is reported descriptively without statistical testing.

title: HistoryLand: a Serious Game for History Learning in Primary Education
study_design: One-shot pre-post questionnaire study (no control group)
statistical_results: Three significant pre-post differences: (1) Pedagogical value of computer-based activities: Z=-1.97, p=0.04, r=-0.24 (pre M=2.84, SD=1.46; post M=3.41, SD=1.42); (2) Concentration levels/distraction: Z=-2.61, p=0.00, r=-0.32 (game M=2.38, SD=1.59 vs typical lesson M=3.25, SD=1.52); (3) Preference for group work: Z=-3.57, p=0.00, r=-0.43 (pre M=3.65, SD=1.54; post M=4.65, SD=0.92). Significant correlations: immersion-enjoyment r=0.914, p=0.000; immersion-knowledge improvement r=0.793, p=0.000; collaboration-knowledge improvement r=0.887, p=0.000.
key_outcomes: Students perceived the game favorably across all four dimensions (enjoyment, immersion, collaboration, knowledge improvement), with all mean scores above 4.0 on a 5-point scale. Students rated computer-supported learning activities as significantly more useful after playing the game. Distraction levels during the game were significantly lower than during typical History lessons. Preference for collaborative group work significantly increased after the game activity.
engagement_results: Enjoyment M=4.41 (SD=0.37); Immersion M=4.18 (SD=0.64); students felt highly involved in the game (M=4.85, SD=0.49); forgot about time passing (M=4.73, SD=0.78); the game grabbed attention (M=4.76, SD=0.76)
comparative_methodology: Pre-post questionnaire comparison using Wilcoxon Signed-ranks test (non-parametric, as normality and homogeneity of variance criteria were not satisfied). No control group comparison.

title: History-Themed Games in History Education: Experiences on a Blended World History Course
key_outcomes: Five key qualitative learning outcomes were observed: (1) In-depth geographical knowledge - students internalized concepts of strategic and economic importance through interactive world maps; (2) Increased awareness of interaction between various societal issues - students became aware of complex interactions between economic, religious, technological, political, and cultural elements; (3) Experience-based immersive learning - students reported a critical immersive component with trial-and-error methodology allowing internalization of historical interactions; (4) Discussion over modeling decisions - students critically engaged with and debated the game's modeling choices (e.g., Eurocentric trade networks, westernization mechanic); (5) Contextualizing key events and major developments - students shifted from modern viewpoints to historical perspectives, understanding events as part of greater processes.
engagement_results: Students who could not achieve assigned goals in game-based assignments self-incentivized to try again with different tactics and decisions, even though success or failure was explicitly stated as unimportant. This self-motivated repetition created high personal motivation and further increased immersiveness. Students also spontaneously initiated critical discussions about game modeling decisions.
comparative_methodology: The authors compared three game series over multiple course iterations (2015-2018): Civilization series, Total War series, and Paradox Grand Strategy series. In the first two years they used one game from each series (Civilization IV, Crusader Kings II, Empire Total War). Based on observations, Grand Strategy games provided the most comprehensive experience due to level of detail, high historical accuracy, and versatility, leading them to switch entirely to Grand Strategy games in later iterations.
game_type: commercial off-the-shelf strategy video games (grand strategy)

title: How a Serious Game Supports Elementary School History Classes in Teaching About the Bombardment of Copenhagen in 1807
explicit_definition: Previous definitions have emphasized that serious games are applications that are not designed exclusively for fun or that are intended to be more than entertainment.
statistical_results: Experimental group answered questions correctly to a much higher degree than control group. Q1: Exp 82% vs Con 9% (diff 73%); Q5: Exp 90% vs Con 20% (diff 70%); Q6: Exp 60% vs Con 0% (diff 60%). However Q2: Exp 0% vs Con 20% (diff -20%). Engagement questionnaire: highest mean score Q2.2 (intuitiveness, Mean: 4.00, SD: 0.943); Q2.3 narrative clarity (Mean: 3.60, SD: 1.174); Q1.2 purpose clarity (Mean: 3.45, SD: 0.820).
key_outcomes: The experimental gaming group showed substantially higher understanding of specific learning objectives compared to the control group on most questions (73%, 70%, and 60% advantages on Q1, Q5, Q6 respectively). The game was perceived as intuitive and the narrative was clear.
engagement_results: Interviews revealed mainly positive perceptions across feedback, immersion, teaching, and motivation themes. 8 positive vs 3 negative statements for feedback; 6 positive vs 5 negative for immersion; 8 positive vs 3 negative for teaching. Students found it 'more fun than the traditional teaching in history class' but some felt 'the game was overloaded with information.'
comparative_methodology: Quasi-experimental comparison between experimental (gaming) group and control (analogue textbook reading) group, with both groups taking the same 6-question knowledge test

title: How Much Life do I Lose from the Plague? Educational Board Games as Teaching Tools in Archaeology and Ancient History Courses
explicit_definition: Abt (1987: 9) defines them as games that have 'an explicit and carefully thought-out educational purpose and are not intended to be played primarily for amusement, but that does not mean they are not, or should not, be entertaining.'
key_outcomes: Overall, from the quality of the final games produced, it is clear that students took their tasks quite seriously and were getting enough out of the project to view it as much more than just another assignment. Student feedback was diverse, but overwhelmingly positive. The educational board gaming project achieved very positive feedback in standard departmental evaluations.
engagement_results: Students took tasks quite seriously and viewed the project as much more than just another assignment. Student feedback was diverse, but overwhelmingly positive. The distinctiveness and success of the project was even noted by the local university media as something that might be emulated.
comparative_methodology: No formal comparative methodology. Assessment centred around three specific criteria: (1) overall success of the game itself; (2) individual and team member participation evaluations; (3) a game overview document. Standard departmental class and teacher evaluation forms were also used.

title: Indonesian History Educational Card Game: Gamification of the Process of Learning to Increase Interest in History among Children
explicit_definition: Gamification is a method of applying game mechanics to engage and motivate people more to complete their task voluntarily. People has a natural desire for competition, achievement, status and collaboration. Gamification is a great method to motivate people to put a greater performance.
statistical_results: Only 22% (13 people) of respondents said they like history; 35% dislike history; 43% feel neutral. 58% (35 people) are interested in a game to help learn history in class; 35% are not sure; 7% are not interested. 72% like playing games; 88% have played board/card games before.
key_outcomes: The survey established a need for gamified history learning. Informal game testing showed: younger students (4th-6th grade) found it somewhat difficult to get answers correct; older students (up to 10th grade) found it noticeably much easier and had fun prompting younger ones to join. Adults had difficulty with correct answers (lessons mostly forgotten) but had fun playing and trying to remember.
engagement_results: 58% of respondents expressed interest in a history learning game. Informal testing showed the card game generated enthusiasm across age groups. Older students 'seemed to have much fun' and prompted younger ones to join. One adult described it as 'an enjoyable way to learn.' The card game was described as offering a 'more visual manner' and 'dynamic, colorful and expressive visuals' compared to text-heavy history books.

title: Investigating elementary students' epistemological beliefs, game preference by applying game-based learning to a history course
study_design: survey-based quantitative study using structural equation modeling (PLS-SEM)
statistical_results: All five hypotheses were confirmed. Perceived ease of use significantly predicted usefulness (0.34) and preference (0.21). Usefulness significantly predicted preference (0.32). Sophisticated epistemological beliefs significantly predicted preference (0.31). Preference significantly predicted intention to use (0.38).
key_outcomes: All TAM hypotheses were confirmed. Perceived usefulness had the strongest influence on game preference among TAM variables. Sophisticated epistemological beliefs positively affected preference for digital games. Preference for digital games positively influenced behavioral intention to use digital game-based learning. Student-centered game-based learning can better attract students than traditional teacher-centered methods.
engagement_results: Game-based learning in history was found to involve a higher level of learning activities and engagements, supported by reference to Cozar-Gutierrez & Saez-Lopez (2016). The role of game features in fostering students' learning and motivation was also confirmed.
game_type: digital history game (custom-designed educational game integrating historical events)

title: Jingnan Campaign©-Using Game-Based Assessment with the Mechanism of Strategy Games for History Teaching: System Development and Learning Evaluation
study_design: pre-experimental (single group pre-post test with survey)
statistical_results: Paired t-test on pre-post test: t = 7.72, p < .05 (significant progress in history knowledge). Post-test correlated with flow antecedent: r = 0.39, p = .037. Post-test correlated with entire flow state: r = 0.37, p = .047. Regression: entire flow state significantly explained variance of post-test (beta = 0.39, p < .05). No significant gender differences in technology acceptance, flow state, or learning achievement.
key_outcomes: Significant learning achievement gains after using the game-based assessment system; positive perceptions of perceived usefulness (mean above median of 3); perceived ease of use slightly below median (M = 2.87); flow state positively associated with learning achievement and explained its variability to a certain extent
engagement_results: Perceived usefulness and flow state means were above the median (3 points), indicating positive engagement. Flow state was significantly positively correlated with learning achievement. Perceived ease of use did not reach the median, possibly due to learners' lack of experience with strategy games.
comparative_methodology: Single group pre-post test comparison (no control group); gender comparison (no significant differences found)

title: Learning About the Past Through Digital Play: History Students and Video Games
study_design: qualitative survey with speculative design fiction
key_outcomes: Students perceived historical video games as powerful tools for learning about history. Key findings: (1) Motivation - students reported intrinsic motivation through agency, empowerment, and immersion in historical settings; interest in specific historical periods was sparked or deepened. (2) Experience - aesthetics, social interaction, choice/agency, and challenge were vital factors for positive gaming experience; games encouraged collaborative and social learning. (3) Learning - students reported learning historical information, engaging in historical/counterfactual thinking, understanding systemic contexts, and being motivated to conduct additional research outside the game. Gameplay extended beyond information acquisition to engagement in processes of historical thinking.
engagement_results: Students reported high engagement through: sense of agency and empowerment ('The plot arc gives a real sense of empowerment'), deep engagement with historical characters/polities, immersion in authentic historical environments, social/collaborative gameplay, replay value through different historical scenarios, and motivation to research topics beyond the game world (online research, books, Wikipedia, visiting places)
game_type: commercial historical video games (various genres including strategy, RPG, action-adventure)

title: Learning Chinese History through Digital Game
statistical_results: Descriptive statistics only (percentages from survey responses). No inferential statistical tests were performed.
key_outcomes: Students reported positive perceptions of game-based learning for history. The majority felt the game improved their learning motivation (74%), that they learned history content from the game (70%), and that they liked this game-based learning approach (81%). Teachers reported positive changes in students' learning attitudes, noting students were more interested and concentrated in class. Teachers indicated they would continue adopting the game-based approach.
engagement_results: 83% of students liked the game. Students commented that 'it attracts me to play', 'it is nice to learn in a happy way', 'we like games, so education mixing games is good', and 'it is easier for me to learn through games'. Teachers observed students were more interested and concentrated during lessons. The game was played over 6336 times in one year on the HKEdCity platform.

title: Learning Cultural Heritage History in Muzium Negara through Role-playing Game
study_design: Design-based research with post-implementation survey evaluation
statistical_results: Descriptive statistics only. Total average mean across all eGameFlow dimensions was 4.24 (84.8%). Highest-rated dimension was Autonomy (4.63); lowest was Feedback (4.10). Individual items ranged from 3.67 (online support for challenges, H4) to 4.84 (sense of control over menu A1, knowing next step A8, sense of control over game A9).
key_outcomes: 84.8% of participants experienced enjoyment while playing the game. The game was identified to efficiently increase knowledge on knowing and memorizing history content in the museum. Autonomy scored highest (4.63), indicating players felt strong sense of control. Knowledge Improvement scored 4.31, suggesting the game enhanced players' knowledge about Malaysia's history.
engagement_results: Concentration mean=4.13; Immersion mean=4.23 (players reported forgetting time, becoming unaware of surroundings, feeling emotionally involved). Challenge mean=4.12. Overall engagement was positive with 84.8% enjoyment rating.

title: Learning History by Playing a Mobile City Game
study_design: Quasi-experimental with mixed methods (quantitative and qualitative)
statistical_results: No statistical results reported; results are described as preliminary. The quantitative data from Pilot 2 had not yet been fully analyzed at the time of writing.
key_outcomes: Preliminary results show high pupil motivation and active engagement in playing and learning about medieval Amsterdam. Pupils were on-task most of the day despite normally having short attention spans. Pupils reported the game was more fun than regular history lessons. Guides reported small knowledge gains (e.g., pupils realizing not every tower is a church). Pupils from pre-university education performed better than those from vocational secondary education. Collaborative skills were developed through the game's team-based structure requiring communication between city teams and HQ teams.
engagement_results: Pupils were very enthusiastic about the game, both at HQ and in the city. Children who normally could not focus for more than 10 minutes were now working concentrated for hours. Most pupils were engaged to complete assignments and on-task most of the day. Qualitative data showed that technical problems caused motivation to decrease, but not always. Pupils at HQ reported they liked HQ even more than walking in the city, as they had a better overview and more control.
comparative_methodology: Quasi-experimental design with experimental condition (10 classes playing Frequency 1550) and control condition (10 classes receiving regular project-based lessons on the medieval history of Amsterdam). Measures taken before intervention, during intervention, immediately after, after 1 week, and after 2 months.

title: Learning History Through Computer Game Authoring
study_design: qualitative case study with interviews and open-ended discussion
key_outcomes: Four out of five participants completed their historical RPGs. Qualitative findings from open-ended discussions and interviews showed: (1) participants found learning history through RPG authoring more enjoyable than traditional methods; (2) participants reported being more engaged with the subject matter; (3) participants viewed the method as innovative and practically engaging; (4) the interaction between participants during presentation and discussion led to different perspectives toward historical events, fostering historical thinking; (5) participants changed their initial storyboard plans during authoring because they generated more ideas during the process, indicating deep engagement with content.
engagement_results: Participants reported positive engagement. Sample comments included: 'I like the latter method; it makes learning history become more enjoyable', 'I am more engaged to the subject being learned', and 'I see it is an innovative way in learning history. It could practically engage me to the topic that I have to learn.' Participants promoted group work and peer collaboration during the workshop.

title: Mobile games to foster the learning of history at archaeological sites
key_outcomes: The pilot usability evaluation provided qualitative design feedback rather than measured learning outcomes. Students preferred audio-enhanced game over silent version, indicating greater engagement. Students identified usability issues: absence of feedback during system delays, unclear functionalities during 3D-reconstruction exploration, and need for digital map on the phone to complement the paper-based map. The authors note that 'the joy and learning efficiency must be established using a more systematic on-site empirical evaluations.' Preliminary studies confirmed the belief that game-play engages students and permits an effective and exciting visit.
engagement_results: Students preferred audio which created greater engagement. The game-play was reported to engage students and permit an effective and exciting visit of the archaeological sites, enhancing the overall students' experience, though this was based on preliminary pilot observations rather than formal measurement.
game_type: mobile excursion-game (treasure hunt-style educational game on cellular phones)

title: Online Interactive Game-Based Learning in High School History Education: Impact on Educational Effectiveness and Student Motivation
study_design: quasi-experimental with pretest-posttest nonequivalent control group design
statistical_results: Experimental group (low achievers): pretest mean=84.1818, posttest mean=91.4545, t(10)=significant at p=.010. Control group (high achievers): pretest mean=94.0263, posttest mean=96.2105, p=.061 (not significant). Experimental group improvement was -7.27 vs control group improvement of -1.68. Questionnaire results: Strongly agree 61.82%, Agree 27.27%, Neutral 10.91%, Disagree 0%, Strongly disagree 0%, grand mean 4.51 out of 5. Over 90% of students approved the system's attraction to participation and intention.
key_outcomes: IGLS significantly improved academic performance for the experimental group (low achievers) at p<.05. The control group showed no significant improvement. IGLS especially provides low achievers with confidence and positive attitude. Over 90% of students showed positive motivation toward using the system. The system enhanced participation, performance improvement, ease of learning, interest in history, and suitability for history learning.
engagement_results: Interface satisfaction: mean scores ranged from 4.55 to 4.82 (easy to handle: 4.64, content clearly expressed: 4.73, buttons easy to click: 4.82, convenience of design: 4.55). Functionality satisfaction: records help with learning 4.55, group competition helps 4.55, online version helps 4.55, message board makes communication easier 4.09, handle situation in group competition 4.45. Motivation improvement: game arouses participation 4.55, improves performance 4.64, eases presence in learning 4.64, attracts interest in history 4.64, system suitable for learning history 4.36.
comparative_methodology: Pretest-posttest comparison between experimental group (using IGLS) and control group (traditional instruction). Pretest result of Taiwan history used as covariance, learning method as independent variable, post test as dependent variable.
game_type: online interactive quiz-based game / web-based competition game

title: Playhist: Play and Learn History. Learning with a Historical Game vs An Interactive Film
study_design: Randomized controlled experiment (two-group comparison: control group watching interactive film vs experimental group playing serious game)
key_outcomes: The paper describes the planned experimental design but does not report final outcome data. The authors conclude theoretically that serious games for cultural heritage are particularly suited to the affective domain, that empathy with game characters helps understanding of historical events, cultures, and heritage, and that 3D Virtual Worlds have the potential to expand knowledge of foreign cultures by presenting information in a visual context.
engagement_results: Not reported (planned to be measured via QoE questionnaires and ECC module automatic data collection)
comparative_methodology: Two-group randomized comparison: Group A (control) watches the existing interactive film at FHW; Group B (experimental) plays the 3D serious game developed with Unity3D. Both groups are assessed using the same QoE and QoL questionnaires for direct comparison.

title: Reliving History with "Reliving the Revolution": Designing Augmented Reality Games to Teach the Critical Thinking of History
study_design: Design-based research with iterative prototyping, qualitative case study with pre- and post-game surveys, videotaped and in-person observations, and content analysis of debates, game discussions, and notes
education_level: Mixed (graduate students, educators, and high school students aged 13-17)
key_outcomes: RtR motivated discovery, enthusiasm, reflection, collaboration, teamwork, problem solving, interpretation, analysis, and consideration of alternative views of history. Participants engaged with historical content, felt immersed in the Battle of Lexington, and practiced historical thinking skills including questioning sources, identifying biases, creating hypotheses, and drawing inferences. The Redesign trial showed improvements: participants were less overwhelmed, more directed by mini-objectives/checkpoints, and more motivated to collaborate inter-role.
