Participants reported the game felt novel and authentic, and they took the 'serious game' very seriously. They reflected on their own interpretations, questioned preconceived notions about the Battle of Lexington, and related historical understanding to broader social issues.
engagement_results: Participants enjoyed being at the actual historic site and using PDAs to integrate virtual information with a real-world context. The game felt novel and authentic. Walking around was 'more engaging and more interactive.' Participants found particular pleasure in kinesthetic learning and discovering information embedded in the environment. They preferred this to sitting in a classroom. The collaborative aspect was highly valued - participants could share ideas, engage in mini-debates, and reflect more deeply on evidence. Some Pilot participants felt overwhelmed by information overload, but Redesign participants with mini-objectives thrived in the nonlinear environment.
comparative_methodology: Comparison between Pilot study design and Redesign trial through iterative design process; pre- and post-game surveys on game play, attitudes toward history, and knowledge of the Revolutionary War

title: Replaying History: Engaging Urban Underserved Students in Learning World History Through Computer Simulation Games
study_design: Qualitative case study within a design experiment methodology
key_outcomes: Students developed deeper understandings of relationships among history, geography, economics, and politics through gameplay. Key learning outcomes included: (1) understanding interconnections between geography, economics, and political systems; (2) developing multi-factor causal explanations for historical phenomena such as colonization (population density, strategic resources, relations with other civilizations, access to trade networks); (3) learning geographic facts (locations of Egypt, Nova Scotia, Greenland); (4) understanding the role of natural resources in civilization development; (5) ability to construct and test historical hypotheticals (e.g., reversing European colonization of the Americas); (6) recognizing that 'you can't separate geography from economics from politics.' Learning was highly interpretive, driven by students' own goals and mediated by classroom discourse. Powerful systemic-level understandings emerged through gameplay for some students (e.g., Tony) only after approximately 30 hours of play.
engagement_results: Engagement was a complex process of appropriation and resistance. Many students initially rejected the activity (days 1-4), finding Civilization III too complex. By day 4, when students realized they could use the game to 'replay history' and explore hypothetical scenarios, they began to appropriate it. Identity was central to engagement - students were most engaged when the game allowed them to express ideas they believed in or investigate questions tied to their identities (e.g., African-American students wanting to reverse colonization and make the Americas African). Motivation was multi-dimensional, occurring at the intersection of personal goals, fantasies, the possibility space of the simulation, desire to learn world history, and social pressure. Failure in the game drove recursive cycles of problem-solving that led to frustration but also engagement and learning.

title: Storification in History education: A mobile game in and about medieval Amsterdam
study_design: qualitative case study with mixed methods (content analysis of game design, observations, coach observation forms with Likert scales, group interviews, media box/log analysis)
key_outcomes: The game evoked a mixture of three types of storification that differently affected students' engagement. Participating in the story evoked high activity but less awareness of the whole story. Constructing the story triggered awareness of the whole story. Receiving the story was least engaged with by students (they often skipped background texts). Both constructing and participating positively affected engagement compared to receiving. HQTs (directors/constructors) were more motivated and concentrated throughout gameplay than CTs (actors/participants). Students generally focused more on completing assignments than understanding the broader narrative.
engagement_results: Students were very active and motivated in making video recordings and enacting sayings. HQTs were more busy, motivated, and concentrated throughout game play compared to CTs. CTs experienced loss of control and overview of the game. Students paid more attention to procedures and technology than to the story line during introductions. Students generally did not read background texts carefully, scrolling to assignments instead.

title: Sustaining mobile learning with pervasive game: An example of cultural history exploration
explicit_definition: A pervasive game (PG) is a mobile game that seamlessly integrates the physical environment with virtual scenarios. According to Walther (2005), a PG implies a mixed-reality gaming space; that is, the gameplay connects the virtual world with the tangible world.
statistical_results: Learning effectiveness: pre-test mean=31.33 (SD=12.65), post-test mean=88.50 (SD=7.44), t=22.46, p<.001 -- significant improvement. Game rules: pre-test m=25.36, post-test m=25.86, t=-0.803, p=.429 (not significant). Game mechanism: pre-test m=23.73, post-test m=23.56, t=0.22, p=.821 (not significant). Game interaction: pre-test m=29.30, post-test m=29.23, t=0.100, p=.921 (not significant). Game content: pre-test m=12.90, post-test m=20.96, t=-9.950, p<.001 (significant).
key_outcomes: Participants showed highly significant improvement in understanding of Provintia history and culture after the pervasive game activity (pre-test 31.33 to post-test 88.50). Participants performed better on geographical (93.3%) and architectural (92.3%) aspects than on historical (89.4%) and cultural (82.7%) aspects. Game content evaluation showed significant improvement, indicating participants gained more understanding of the site. Game rules, mechanism, and interaction aspects showed no significant differences, meaning the game met participants' expectations in these areas.
engagement_results: Participants reported feeling excited and happy when able to solve riddles, which enhanced their sense of achievement. AR storytelling was noted as making site exploration more interesting. Participants said they would cooperate and share with group members and preferred AR content over textual tourist sign descriptions. The bingo Q&A competition at the end was effective for refreshing memories. Facebook was used for group cooperation, information management, and sharing, though participants preferred shorthand note-taking over smartphone typing.
comparative_methodology: One-group pretest-posttest design with paired t-tests to compare pre- and post-test scores on both learning effectiveness and game effectiveness evaluation

title: Teaching History in an Age of Pervasive Computing: The Case for Games in the High School and Undergraduate Classroom
study_design: Qualitative descriptive / practitioner reflection with case examples
key_outcomes: The chapter presents qualitative case evidence rather than measured outcomes. Key reported observations include: (1) Civfanatics community members engaged in sustained peer review of historical mods for Civilization IV, debating historical accuracy (e.g., Crusades scenario with detailed discussions about religious denominations, territorial boundaries, and historical figures); (2) Undergraduate students in a 2007/08 course successfully designed and built original history games about the War of 1812 using C++ and OpenGL, including Brigade: A War of 1812 Saga and Tavern Keeper; (3) Student reflections noted that game development allowed them to combine political and social history perspectives and express nuanced micro-histories; (4) Students initially resisted game-based assessment (preferring traditional essays) due to unfamiliarity with grading criteria; (5) Augmented reality games (Niagara 1812) demonstrated potential for blending virtual and real-world historical spaces.
engagement_results: Students showed enthusiasm for game development but also experienced anxiety about unfamiliar assessment formats. The Civfanatics community demonstrated high voluntary engagement with historical content through modding, with peer review processes emerging organically. Students were reluctant to replace traditional essays with game diaries in first-year courses.
game_type: Commercial strategy games (Civilization IV, Caesar IV), game mods/scenarios, student-built games (ex novo), augmented reality games, web-based games (The Nethernet/PMOG)

title: Teaching History With Custom-Built Board Games
study_design: qualitative pilot study with mixed-methods data collection (anonymous feedback forms with Likert-scale ratings, facilitator observation, and external observation)
statistical_results: Descriptive statistics only. Mean enjoyability rating: 4.7 out of 5. Mean historical argument clarity rating: 4.5 out of 5. No inferential statistics or significance testing was conducted.
key_outcomes: Student participation and understanding of historical context improved during the game. Custom-built board games increase student participation and teach not only historical content (facts, names, dates) but also complex ideas such as research methodologies and historical empathy. Groups resolved confusion more efficiently than individuals. Time-constrained decision-making helped maintain engagement. Inability to win did not cause disengagement in short games. Structured debriefing was essential for achieving educational goals.
engagement_results: External observers noted that by the second round, every student appeared engaged; only one student did not engage during the first round. High levels of engagement in the debrief after the game exceeded other activities attempted in the course (primary source readings, short movie clips). Increased participation during the game did not last beyond the game session itself. Graduate and undergraduate students showed similar enjoyment and belief in historical argument quality, but curricular differences influenced how each group approached the game.
comparative_methodology: Comparison between graduate (n=7 from one observed session, n=18 total) and undergraduate (n=28 from one observed session, n=70 total) student responses. Also a survey question comparing game effectiveness to traditional lecture. No formal control group.

title: Teaching history with the video game Assassin’s Creed: effective teaching practices and reported learning
study_design: exploratory mixed-methods case study (questionnaires, individual and group interviews, videotaped classroom observations; quantitative descriptive/inferential statistics via SPSS 22 and qualitative content analysis)
statistical_results: Significant gender differences in playing and liking Assassin's Creed (boys > girls). Significant differences in student appreciation across teachers: T1 (illustration-only approach) rated significantly lower than T2, T3, T4 (historical thinking approach). ANOVA results all at p<.01 level.
key_outcomes: Five categories of student-reported learning: events (n=205), characters (n=63), places (n=33), monuments and buildings (n=33), cultures (n=13). Almost all learning was declarative knowledge. Students reported increased motivation, engagement, and interest in history. The multimedia aspects of video games (images, music, cinematics) served as effective learning vectors. Students reported feeling immersed and that the game helped them make connections between school content and outside knowledge. Teaching practices that fostered historical/critical thinking (T2-T4) were significantly more appreciated and effective than illustration-only approaches (T1).
engagement_results: 59% of students found classroom use of AC very interesting or loved it. 52% wished it were used more. Students reported increased curiosity and motivation: 'It makes me feel like learning more about the subject,' 'It's more fun to learn history.' Students described feeling 'almost there' and immersed. The game had direct repercussions on classroom behavior: 'I tend to listen more when it's more interesting.' 54% had already played the game and felt a home-school connection.
comparative_methodology: Cross-teacher comparison of four teachers' different pedagogical approaches to using Assassin's Creed: T1 used lecture-style illustration (screenshots, clips as visual support without critical comparison); T2, T3, T4 used dialectic/investigative inquiry approach (comparing game content with other historical sources, fostering historical thinking). Students rated T2-T4 approaches significantly higher.
game_type: commercial off-the-shelf (COTS) video game used as educational resource (not directly played by students in class)

title: The "Architectural Jewels of Lublin" Game as a Tool for Collaborative Interactive Learning of History
study_design: Survey-based descriptive study with game design presentation
statistical_results: Hypothesis H1 confirmed: average knowledge level of K14 pupils about Lublin architectural monuments is very low (around 20-23%). Hypothesis H2 confirmed: knowledge levels do not substantially differ between Lublin residents and non-residents. No student exceeded the 50% threshold.
key_outcomes: K14 pupils have very low knowledge of Lublin's architectural monuments and their history, confirming the need for the educational game. The game itself was not empirically tested for learning effectiveness in this study; this is listed as future work.
comparative_methodology: Comparison between two groups (Lublin residents vs. non-residents, 12 pupils each) on the same knowledge test using weighted scores across 7 monuments and 3 question types (name, time period, architectural style). Descriptive statistics (mean, median, min, max, standard deviation) and histograms were used.
game_type: Technology-enhanced board game with 3D printed models, RFID sensing, and palmtop software

title: The Development and Evaluation of an Online Educational Game Integrated with Real Person-NPC mechanism for History Learning
statistical_results: Wilcoxon signed rank test for learning performance: pre-test M=5.50, SD=3.63; post-test M=9.00, SD=3.54; Z=-2.77, p=.006 (p<.01). Overall flow score M=4.23, SD=0.49. Flow antecedents M=4.18, SD=0.58 (Challenge M=4.17, SD=0.91; Goal M=4.25, SD=0.54; Feedback M=3.88, SD=0.88; Control M=4.42, SD=0.51; Playability M=4.17, SD=0.89). Flow experience M=4.28, SD=0.46 (Concentration M=4.50, SD=0.55; Time distortion M=4.33, SD=0.49; Autotelic experience M=4.54, SD=0.53; Loss of self-consciousness M=3.29, SD=1.05).
key_outcomes: Significant improvement in learners' knowledge of history and capabilities of strategic planning after playing the game (pre-test M=5.50 to post-test M=9.00, Z=-2.77, p=.006). The authors state: 'learners' knowledge of history and the capabilities of strategic planning improved through this game.'
engagement_results: High flow state reported: overall flow M=4.23 (above median of 3 on 5-point scale). Highest sub-dimension scores: Autotelic experience M=4.54, Concentration M=4.50, Control M=4.42. Lowest: Loss of self-consciousness M=3.29, Feedback M=3.88. The authors conclude: 'learners were deeply involved in the game.'
comparative_methodology: Single-group pre-test/post-test design using Wilcoxon signed rank test (non-parametric) to compare learning performance before and after game-based intervention. No control group.

title: The Development of a Role-Playing Game for History Instruction and the Evaluation of Flow State and Learning Performance
statistical_results: Paired-samples t test results: History score: post-test M=12.58, SD=1.32; pre-test M=6.55, SD=2.28; t=15.52, p=.000 (p<0.001). Geography score: post-test M=2.58, SD=1.11; pre-test M=1.75, SD=1.03; t=4.62, p=.000 (p<0.001). Flow questionnaire results: Overall flow antecedents M=4.06, SD=0.62; challenge-skills balance M=3.96, SD=0.87; goals of an activity M=4.11, SD=0.75; unambiguous feedback M=3.91, SD=0.74; control M=4.18, SD=0.78; action-awareness merging M=4.13, SD=0.76. Overall flow experience M=3.82, SD=0.64; concentration M=3.85, SD=0.75; transformation of time M=3.68, SD=0.79; autotelic experience M=3.66, SD=0.77; loss of self-consciousness M=4.24, SD=0.80.
key_outcomes: Significant improvement in both history knowledge (pre-test M=6.55 to post-test M=12.58, t=15.52, p<.001) and geographical location knowledge (pre-test M=1.75 to post-test M=2.58, t=4.62, p<.001) after game-based learning. The authors state: 'after game-based learning, students' knowledge of history (t=15.52, p=.000) and knowledge related to geographical location (t=4.62, p=.000) were significantly improved.'
engagement_results: All flow dimensions scored above the median of 3.00 on the 5-point Likert scale. Flow antecedents (M=4.06) and flow experience (M=3.82) both above median. Four dimensions scored above 4.00: flow antecedents overall, goals of an activity, control, action-awareness merging, and loss of self-consciousness. The highest scoring dimension was loss of self-consciousness (M=4.24, SD=0.80). The authors conclude: 'this game has the elements to arouse learner's flow experience as a whole' and 'the content of this game can arouse learners' engagement to a certain degree.'
comparative_methodology: Single-group pre-test/post-test design using paired-samples t test to compare learning performance before and after the game-based intervention. No control group.

title: The Development of History Educational Game as a Revision Tool for Malaysia School Education
explicit_definition: An educational game, one designed for learning, is a subset of both play and fun. It is a melding of educational content, learning principles, and computer games [13]. An educational game is combining the element of joy and learns in a playable situation.
statistical_results: Perceived Usefulness (7-point scale): Question 1 Mean=6.25, SE=0.25, Median=7, Mode=7; Question 2 Mean=5.9, SE=0.26, Median=6, Mode=7; Question 3 Mean=5.31, SE=0.41, Median=6, Mode=6; Question 4 Mean=5.75, SE=0.28, Median=6, Mode=7; Question 5 Mean=5.8, SE=0.32, Median=6.5, Mode=7; Question 6 Mean=6.31, SE=0.26, Median=7, Mode=7. Ease of Use: Question 7 Mean=5.15, SE=0.43, Median=5, Mode=7; Question 8 Mean=4.57, SE=0.53, Median=6, Mode=7; Question 9 Mean=5.85, SE=0.34, Median=6, Mode=7; Question 10 Mean=5.63, SE=0.32, Median=6, Mode=7; Question 11 Mean=5.2, SE=0.40, Median=6, Mode=6; Question 12 Mean=5.89, SE=0.43, Median=7, Mode=7.
key_outcomes: The average score from the prototype is around 4.5 to 6.3 on a 7-point scale. The authors state: 'From the result we can concluded that the average score from the prototype is around 4.5 to 6.3. This is because the users are unfamiliar with the game environment and new to the system. The median of every question is around five to seven.' The highest rated item was Question 6 (perceived usefulness, M=6.31) and the lowest was Question 8 (ease of use, M=4.57). From user feedback, 'the most positive aspect is about the effectiveness of the game to help the users to revise the history subject. They can revise the subject quickly and much more fun compare to the conventional methods.'
engagement_results: From qualitative feedback: 'the most positive aspect is about the effectiveness of the game to help the users to revise the history subject. They can revise the subject quickly and much more fun compare to the conventional methods.' However, 'the most negative aspect is the violent and the use of gun in the game and it's not really appreciated by the users.' The perceived usefulness scores (M range 5.31-6.31) were generally higher than ease of use scores (M range 4.57-5.89), suggesting the game was seen as useful but somewhat difficult to use.
comparative_methodology: No comparative methodology; single-group descriptive survey design with no control group or pre-post comparison. Only a post-use PUEU questionnaire was administered.

title: The Effect of the Game-Based Learning Model on Student Engagement in History Learning
statistical_results: One-way ANOVA: F(1,64) = 4.408, p = .040 < .05, Mean Square Between Groups = 87.515, Mean Square Within Groups = 19.853. LSD follow-up test results: Control Pre-test vs Control Post-test: Mean Difference (I-J) = -9.57576*, Std. Error = 1.18233, Sig. = .013; Control Pre-test vs Experimental Pre-test: Mean Difference = .12121, Std. Error = 1.18233, Sig. = .893; Control Pre-test vs Experimental Post-test: Mean Difference = -12.03030*, Std. Error = 1.18233, Sig. = .000; Experimental Pre-test vs Control Post-test: Mean Difference = -9.69697*, Std. Error = 1.18233, Sig. = .000; Experimental Pre-test vs Experimental Post-test: Mean Difference = -12.15152*, Std. Error = 1.18233, Sig. = .020. Normality test (Kolmogorov-Smirnov): control class post-questionnaire significance = 0.066 > 0.05 (normal); experimental class post-questionnaire significance = 0.200 > 0.05 (normal). Homogeneity test (Levene's Statistic): significance = 0.069; Levene's significance = 0.793 > 0.05. Ftable at df=65, alpha=0.05 is 3.989; Fcount (4.408) > Ftable (3.989).
key_outcomes: The one-way ANOVA test showed a significant influence on student engagement when students were taught using the game-based learning model (F=4.408, p=0.040<0.05). The LSD follow-up test showed a mean difference (I-J) of 2.45455 between the experimental post-test and control post-test with a significance value of 0.069 > 0.05. The experimental group taught using the game-based learning model had better student engagement effect than the control group taught using the discovery learning model.
engagement_results: The experimental group (GBL with Quizizz) showed significantly higher student engagement than the control group (discovery learning). Several engagement indicators had highest averages: Statement 7 'I will arrive at school before the bell rings' (avg 121.5); Statement 17 'I respect all teachers in this school' and Statement 18 'all teachers must be respected' (avg 121.5); Statement 29 'I will record all the lessons delivered by the teacher' (avg 121); Statement 20 'even though we students are different, we should respect each other' (avg 119); Statement 4 'when the teacher explains the lesson, I fully concentrate on understanding the material' (avg 117.5); Statement 2 'I look for information in other media if I struggle with schoolwork' (avg 117); Statement 8 'all the attributes on my school uniform' (avg 116.5). The GBL model increased student engagement across all three indicators: behavioral, emotional, and cognitive engagement.
comparative_methodology: Quasi-experimental design with a post-test-only non-equivalent control-group design. Experimental group (XI IPS 1, n=33) received game-based learning model assisted by Quizizz application; control group (XI IPS 4, n=33) received discovery learning model. Groups were selected based on homogeneity test of average daily test scores. Comparison via one-way ANOVA with LSD follow-up test at 5% significance level.

title: The Effects of Online Interactive Games on High School Students' Achievement and Motivation in History Learning
explicit_definition: DGBL was first proposed by Marc Prensky in 2001. Through digital games, learners obtain sense of achievement in solving problems and dealing with challenges. Digital game based learning takes both entertainment and education into consideration.
statistical_results: Paired sample t test (Table 2): Control group pretest-posttest: Mean difference = -1.68421, SD = 3.66746, SEM = .84137, 95% CI [-3.45187, .08345], t = -2.002, df = 18, Significance (Two-Tailed) = .061. Experimental group pretest-posttest: Mean difference = -7.27273, SD = 7.55104, SEM = 2.27672, 95% CI [-12.34558, -2.19987], t = -3.194, df = 10, Significance (Two-Tailed) = .010. Descriptive statistics (Table 1): Control group Pretest1 Mean = 94.5263, N = 19, SD = 3.04354, SEM = .69824; Control group Posttest1 Mean = 96.2105, N = 19, SD = 2.57291, SEM = .59027; Experimental group Pretest2 Mean = 84.1818, N = 11, SD = 3.51620, SEM = 1.06017; Experimental group Posttest2 Mean = 91.4545, N = 11, SD = 10.04354, SEM = 3.02824. ANCOVA Table 3 (Gender): F = .163, p = not significant; gender F = .098; R Squared = .405 (Adjusted R Squared = .235), p < .05. ANCOVA Table 4 (Weekly time surfing the Net): F = .786; weekly time surfing the Net F = .821; R Squared = .152 (Adjusted R Squared = -.272), p < .05. ANCOVA Table 5 (Affection network leisure type): F = .171; affection network leisure type F = .130; R Squared = .541 (Adjusted R Squared = .312), p < .05. ANCOVA Table 6 (Login IGLS per week): F = .059; Login IGLS per week F(2,6) = 5.687, p = .041; R Squared = .687 (Adjusted R Squared = .531), p < .05.
key_outcomes: The experimental group (low achievers using IGLS) showed statistically significant improvement from pretest to posttest (mean improvement of 7.27 points, t = -3.194, p = .010), while the control group (high achievers without IGLS) did not reach significance (mean improvement of 1.68 points, t = -2.002, p = .061). ANCOVA showed that only the number of days logging into IGLS per week had a significant effect on post-test scores (F = 5.687, p = .041), with R Squared = .687. Gender, weekly time surfing the Net, and affection network leisure type did not significantly affect post-test scores.
engagement_results: IGLS Questionnaire results (Likert 5-point scale): Interface satisfaction (Table 7): 'The interface is easy to handle' Mean = 4.64, SD = 0.505; 'The content is clearly expressed' Mean = 4.73, SD = 0.467; 'The buttons are easy to click on' Mean = 4.82, SD = 0.405; 'Convenience of the design' Mean = 4.55, SD = 0.688. Function satisfaction (Table 8): 'The records do help me with learning' Mean = 4.55, SD = 0.688; 'The group competition help me with learning' Mean = 4.55, SD = 0.688; 'The online version help me with learning' Mean = 4.55, SD = 0.522; 'The message board makes communication easier for me' Mean = 4.09, SD = 0.831; 'I can handle the situation in group competition' Mean = 4.45, SD = 0.820. Motivation satisfaction (Table 9): 'The game arouses my participation' Mean = 4.55, SD = 0.688; 'The game improves my performance' Mean = 4.64, SD = 0.505; 'The game eases my pressure in learning' Mean = 4.64, SD = 0.674; 'The game attracts my interest in history' Mean = 4.36, SD = 0.809; 'I think the system is suitable for learning history' Mean = 4.36, SD = 0.809. Grand mean = 4.51. Over ninety percent students approve of the system's attraction to their participation and intension. Result distribution: strongly agree (61.82%), agree (27.27%), neutral (10.91%), disagree (0%), strongly disagree (0%).
comparative_methodology: Quasi-experimental design with non-equivalent groups. Control group (n=19, high achievers with pretest scores above average of 90) and experimental group (n=11, low achievers with pretest scores below average of 90). Four-week experiment. Pre-test of Taiwan history (Vol. 1) used as covariate in ANCOVA analyses. Post-test scores used as dependent variable. Paired sample t-test used to compare pretest-posttest improvement within each group.

title: The Evaluation Study of Gamification Approach in Malaysian History Learning via Mobile Game Application
key_outcomes: Qualitative evaluation results from focus group: User Experience (UX) -- 'The UX is rather lackluster, due to lack of animations and disjointed graphics and themes' (needs improvement); Story -- 'The story is consistent with the syllabus, and follows a narrative flow. Each chapter has its own unique narrative' (excellent); Gameplay Complexity -- 'Simple, using only touch inputs. Challenges are easy to comprehend and overcome' (sufficient); Estimated Average Play Session -- '8-20 minutes, depending on familiarity of the chapter' (excellent); Engagement -- 'High engagement. Supported by natural flow of story and challenges' (sufficient); Historical Content Delivered -- 'Very high. Due to the game designed around delivering the content of history syllabus to the student' (excellent). Game validation confirmed all five research objectives were met (all passed).
engagement_results: Engagement was rated as 'High engagement. Supported by natural flow of story and challenges' and deemed 'sufficient for the effectiveness level of HLMG.' However, the authors note that 'HLMG has obvious flaws and short comings in graphics which in turns it influences the level of engagement.' The implicit engagement and motivation triggered by learning contents and gamification features were identified as vital for maximising thinking skills during the history learning process.
comparative_methodology: Focus group evaluation with 5 students using a 9-item questionnaire assessing six criteria: user experience (UX), story, gameplay complexity, estimated average play session, engagement, and historical content delivered. Results were qualitative descriptive judgments rather than quantitative measures. The game's final prototype was also compared to similar games (though details of comparison games are not provided).

title: The Game-based Learning Activity Integrating Board Game and Mobile Online Searching Tasks for History Learning
statistical_results: Perceived learning process (Initiate Game Playing Stage vs. Mobile Devices Intervention Stage): Attention: M=3.41 (SD=1.281) vs. M=3.80 (SD=1.135), t=-2.776, p<0.05; Cognitive Engagement: M=2.88 (SD=1.170) vs. M=3.43 (SD=1.304), t=-2.907, p<0.05; Discussion within Groups: M=3.68 (SD=1.336) vs. M=4.08 (SD=1.070), t=-2.722, p<0.05; Usefulness of History Learning: M=3.45 (SD=1.240) vs. M=3.74 (SD=1.159), t=-2.191, p<0.05. Flow state scores (all above 3.0 median): Challenge M=3.85 (SD=0.81); Goal M=4.06 (SD=0.74); Feedback M=3.73 (SD=0.80); Control M=3.77 (SD=0.92); Playability M=3.47 (SD=0.76); Concentration M=3.84 (SD=0.77); Time distortion M=3.87 (SD=1.06); Autotelic experience M=3.85 (SD=0.84); Loss of self-consciousness M=3.09 (SD=0.99).
key_outcomes: Students at the mobile devices intervention stage had significantly higher perceived attention, cognitive engagement, discussion within group, and usefulness of history learning compared with the initial game playing stage (all p<0.05). Students demonstrated flow scores higher than 3.0 (the median of the five-point Likert-type scale) across all nine flow dimensions, indicating high overall flow experience during the combined board game and mobile device activity.
engagement_results: Students demonstrated high flow experience when playing the board game combined with mobile devices, with all nine flow dimensions scoring above the scale median (3.0). The highest flow dimension was Goal (M=4.06), followed by Time distortion (M=3.87), Challenge and Autotelic experience (both M=3.85), Concentration (M=3.84), Control (M=3.77), Feedback (M=3.73), Playability (M=3.47), and Loss of self-consciousness (M=3.09). Discussion within group also increased significantly from M=3.68 to M=4.08 when mobile devices were introduced.
comparative_methodology: Within-subjects comparison of two stages of the same game activity: Stage 1 (initial game playing stage, 9 minutes, board game only) vs. Stage 2 (mobile devices intervention stage, 1 minute, board game with mobile device online searching). Paired t-tests were used to compare perceived learning process scores between the two stages. Flow experience was assessed descriptively by comparing all dimension means against the scale median (3.0).

title: The Pedagogical Application of Alternate Reality Games: Using Game-Based Learning to Revisit History
explicit_definition: Alternate Reality Games (ARGs) are cross media narrative-based games that use the Internet as a central communications platform. The interactions of participants drive the progression and direction of the story and play experience. Boundaries between reality and fiction are disguised, as game designers ensure that the characters and scenarios react dynamically to player input. Working collaboratively, players collate a fragmented narrative by deciphering codes and clues.
statistical_results: The results of the comparative analysis indicated that all twenty-five players improved their knowledge. Indeed, all players showed a noteworthy increase in their post-ARG percentage scores with improvements of knowledge in Players 7, 30, 18 and 21 increasing significantly by 600%, 814%, 1020% and 1800% respectively.
key_outcomes: All 25 players improved their knowledge of the 1916 Easter Rising after playing the ARG. Some players showed dramatic improvements (600%-1800% increases in knowledge percentage scores). The qualitative thematic analysis identified four key evaluation criteria that contributed to successful learning: Assessment, Feedback, Collaborative Learning, and Debriefing. Each of the 23 players who completed the follow-up Questionnaire E agreed with the interim evaluation criterion on Assessment.
engagement_results: Players were highly engaged with the collaborative, narrative-driven ARG. Key engagement factors identified through thematic analysis include: (1) The rewarding aspect of completing challenges 'sufficiently motivated and engaged players to continue playing, whilst also aiding the retention of information'; (2) Diversity of challenges retained player interest, bringing 'freshness' to the game; (3) Collaborative play enhanced focus and attentiveness -- players reported it was 'a lot better than classroom learning' and that they were 'more alert' than 'sitting down with a textbook'; (4) The TINAG philosophy successfully blurred fact/fiction boundaries, with players stating 'I thought Lucy Reilly was real. I couldn't really distinguish between what was fact and what was fiction'; (5) Feedback system motivated continued play and learning.
comparative_methodology: Pre-post comparison of knowledge questionnaire scores administered before and after the ARG game play. No control group. Questionnaire A gathered quantitative data (pre- and post-game test results). A benchmarking system was devised between the researcher and the teachers to maintain consistency and reliability. Qualitative data was collected through participant-observation, Questionnaire C (enjoyment/learning factors), Questionnaire E (follow-up validation of evaluation criteria), and eight focus groups involving 3-4 participants per session, ranging from 40-75 minutes.

title: The Utilization of History Module in the Development of Multiculturalism-Based Team Games Tournament Model to Improve the Bhineka Attitudes on 10th Grade Students in SMA Erlangga Pematangsiantar
statistical_results: Independent sample t test (cognitive): t_count > t_table (3.101 > 1.711) so H0 is rejected and H1 is accepted, indicating a difference in the mean cognitive scores of the experimental and control group students. Independent sample t test (attitude scale): t_count > t_table (2.527 > 1.711) so H0 is rejected and H1 is accepted, indicating diversity attitudes of students who use the history module are higher than students who use conventional models. Paired sample t test (cognitive domain, experimental group): t_count (-6.271) < -t_table (-1.711), H0 rejected. Paired sample t test (affective domain, experimental group): t_count (-3.698) < -t_table (-1.711), H0 rejected. Paired Samples Test (attitude scale, experimental group): Mean difference = -1.542, SD = 2.043, t = -3.698, df = 23, Sig. (2-tailed) = .001. Paired Samples Test (attitude scale, control group): Mean difference = -2.208, SD = 2.187, t = -4.948, df = 23, Sig. (2-tailed) = .000. Kolmogorov-Smirnov normality test: Pre-questionnaire significance = 0.230, Post-questionnaire significance = 0.885. Expert validation: content component average score = 8.8, language component average score = 8.6, total average = 8.7 ('Highly Valid'). Normality test significance values: X1 (post-test A) = 0.305, Y1 (post-questionnaire A) = 0.885, X2 (post-test B) = 0.367, Y2 (post-questionnaire B) = 0.327. Homogeneity test for post-test (cognitive) = 0.5.
key_outcomes: Students using the multiculturalism-based TGT history module showed significantly higher cognitive scores and diversity attitudes compared to students using conventional models. The experimental group showed significant pre-to-post improvement in both cognitive domain (paired t = -6.271) and affective domain (paired t = -3.698, p = .001). The control group also showed significant pre-to-post improvement in attitude scores (paired t = -4.948, p = .000). The expert-validated module achieved 'Highly Valid' status with an average score of 8.7 out of 10.
comparative_methodology: Quasi-experimental design with experimental group (n=24, using multiculturalism-based TGT history module) and control group (n=24, Class X IPA, using conventional models). Independent sample t-tests compared between-group differences on cognitive scores and attitude scale scores. Paired sample t-tests compared within-group pre-post differences for both the experimental and control groups. Normality verified via Kolmogorov-Smirnov and Shapiro-Wilk tests; homogeneity verified via Levene's Variance Homogeneity Test. Statistical analysis performed using SPSS Version 19.

title: Towards an Online Multiplayer Serious Game Providing a Joyful Experience in Learning Art History
explicit_definition: The term Serious Game describes a game designed for a primary purpose other than pure entertainment.
key_outcomes: Only informal usability feedback from a test session with 4 participants is reported. The test 'showed first positive results concerning the style of the game level and the presentation of the learning content.' No formal learning outcomes were measured.
engagement_results: The usability test showed 'first positive results concerning the style of the game level and the presentation of the learning content.' Players provided qualitative feedback about navigation difficulties due to limited house textures and HUD obstructing the view of paintings.
comparative_methodology: The paper describes a planned future evaluation: 'We will split up the test group into an experimental group that plays the game, and a control group that is taught using prevalent methods such as classroom teaching. In the end, both results will be compared to get an insight in the learning success of ThIATRO.' However, this evaluation had not yet been conducted at the time of publication.

title: Using Learning Games to Teach Texas Civil War History to Public Middle School Students
statistical_results: Overall learning gain: text packet group showed 3.7 point improvement; game group showed 2.6 point improvement. One-tailed t-test: p = 0.91, t = 1.76 (no significant difference favoring game). Fischer's exact test on individual questions: Question 5 ('What strategy did the Confederate forces use to attack Galveston during the second battle of Galveston?') showed statistically significant difference favoring game, p = .0007. Mann Whitney U test on Likert data: 'share this learning tool with a friend' -- p = 0.002, U = 58.5, Cohen's d = 1.112 (between large and very large effect); 'interested in learning about the Civil War' -- p = 0.065, U = 93.5, effect size = 0.553 (medium); 'interested in learning about history' -- p = 0.075, U = 95.5, effect size = 0.525 (medium).
key_outcomes: The game did not produce significantly greater overall learning gains compared to the text packet. However, the question most closely tied to the gameplay (Question 5, about Confederate attack strategy in the second Battle of Galveston) showed a statistically significant learning gain for game players (p = .0007). Game players also reported significantly higher likelihood of sharing the learning tool with a friend (p = 0.002, Cohen's d = 1.112) and marginally higher interest in learning about the Civil War (p = 0.065) and history generally (p = 0.075).
engagement_results: Game participants reported statistically significantly higher likelihood of wanting to share the learning tool with a friend (p = 0.002, U = 58.5, Cohen's d = 1.112). Game participants reported marginally significantly higher interest in learning about the Civil War (p = 0.065, U = 93.5, effect size = 0.553) and in learning about history (p = 0.075, U = 95.5, effect size = 0.525). The authors note: 'The sole experience of getting to play in class greatly excited the students, whose enthusiasm seems to extend to a greater interest in the subject material.'
comparative_methodology: Randomized experimental design comparing game group (n=17) vs. text packet control group (n=16). Students were randomly assigned based on seating. Both groups took the same pretest and posttest. One-tailed t-test was used for overall learning gain comparison; Fischer's exact test was used for question-by-question analysis; one-tailed Mann Whitney U test was used for ordinal Likert scale interest data.

title: Using the Rutgers Oral History Archives and Historical Games to Teach Undergraduates Concepts in American Immigration History
key_outcomes: No formal assessment of learning outcomes is reported. The author makes anecdotal claims about the activity's value, stating: 'Not only does the "European Immigration Game" pique student interest in immigration history in a tactile way, but it allows a real assessment of student research and writing skills in the process.' The author also claims: 'core concepts and events in American immigration history can be conveyed, and more importantly, assessed in a tangible way.' However, no empirical evidence (test scores, survey data, student work analysis) is provided to substantiate these claims.
engagement_results: No formal engagement data collected. The author makes qualitative claims that the activity is engaging: 'Of the greatest value, of course, is that undergraduate students are actively engaged with a rich archive of primary source material in an enjoyable way.' No student survey, interview, or observational data is reported.

title: Validity of a Simulation Game as a Method for History Teaching
explicit_definition: The simulation game, as opposed to the role-playing game, does not try to provoke certain feelings in the participant, but rather places him in a context, with certain givens, where he must attempt to increase his chances of winning and decrease his chances of losing. Givens and results are more explicit in a simulation game than in a role-playing game.
statistical_results: Table 2.1 - Test of Historical Knowledge: No significant difference between experimental groups (Group 1, M = 17.42; Group 2, M = 15.65) and control group (Group 0, M = 16.86), F = 0.912, p = .410 (n = 31 experimental vs control). Table 2.2 - Historical Comprehension Test 1: Experimental groups had significantly better results (max = 5.00; Group 1, M = 2.67; Group 2, M = 3.24) than control group (Group 0, M = 1.73), F = 5.578, p = .007 (n = 44). Second comprehension test favored experimental groups but not significantly (Group 1, M = 2.42; Group 2, M = 2.29; Group 0, M = 1.87). Table 2.3 - Historical Knowledge: Formal vs Preformal Students (experimental groups only): Intergroup F = 8.84, p = .006 (Preformal n = 19, M = 15.47, SD = 3.37; Formal n = 14, M = 19.41, SD = 3.80). Formal level as predictor of historical knowledge: r = .53, p = .049, n = 21. No significant difference between formal and preformal for comprehension tests: r = .23, p = .614, n = 21. Involvement and historical comprehension: r = .50, p = .011. Sensorimotor learning style and motivation: Spearman rho = .4297, p = .009. Table 3 correlations: Proprioceptive cinematic and second chance rho = .5011, p = .003; Proprioceptive temporal rho = .4519, p = .007; Sensorimotor rho = .5686, p = .001; Kinesthetic rho = .4674, p = .005; Transactional rho = .4485, p = .007; Auditive and absenteeism rho = .4560, p = .006. Table 4.1: Proportion chi-squared = 0, significance level = 1; Combination chi-squared = 0.13, significance level = .91. Table 5 - Opinions by attitude: Opinion A chi-squared = 9.20, p < .01; Opinion B chi-squared = 15.13, p < .01; Opinion C chi-squared = 10.89, p < .01.
key_outcomes: Experimental groups had significantly higher scores on the first comprehension test (p = .007) compared to the control group. No significant difference on historical knowledge test (p = .410), meaning the game was as efficient as lectures for knowledge acquisition. Within experimental groups, formal students scored significantly higher on knowledge (M = 19.41 vs M = 15.47, p = .006). The game benefited preformal students most in terms of comprehension (no significant difference between formal and preformal on comprehension). The game motivated certain learning styles (sensory-motor, kinesthetic). 64.7% of students found the game more motivating and diversified than a lecture course.
engagement_results: 64.7% found the game more motivating and more diversified than a lecture course; 20.6% found it equally motivating and 23.4% found it equally diversified; 97.1% thought it required an equal or less amount of work than other courses (less work: 55.9%; equal work: 41.2%). The only significant relationship between attitude variables and historical comprehension test results was involvement (r = .50, p = .011). Active involvement was the only affective factor significantly linked to learning. Students preferring sensory-motor learning found the course more motivating (Spearman rho = .4297, p = .009). Proprioceptive, sensorimotor, kinesthetic, and transactional learners enjoyed being able to study abstract matter with tools appropriate to their styles. A great majority would take the course again and thought more than 51% of their peers enjoyed the simulation game.
comparative_methodology: Quasi-experimental design with two experimental groups (simulation game) and one control group (regular lectures) in a History of International Relations course. Three CEGEP-level classes were used: two experimental classes in Drummondville and one control class in Trois-Rivieres. All groups received developmental and learning tests at different times during the term. Control group attended ordinary lectures while experimental groups participated in the simulation game with four scenarios of increasing difficulty. Both groups completed the objective knowledge test and comprehension tests at end of term.

title: Virtual Reality and Educational Game to Learn Madurese History and Alphabet For Elementary School Students
statistical_results: Media design expert validation: 91% (Very High). Material/content expert validation: 84% (High). Individual trial (three 3rd grade students): 85% (High). Small group trial (six 3rd grade students): 87% (High). Large group trial (twenty 3rd grade students): 86% (High). Percentage formula used: Percentage of answers = F/N x 100%, where F = The total value of the respondents, N = Total the maximum value.
key_outcomes: All feasibility scores were in the 'High' or 'Very High' category (84-91%), indicating the product was deemed well worth it with no need to revise. The media design expert gave the highest rating at 91% (Very High). The authors concluded that 'the virtual reality and educational games are well worth it and no need to revise' and that 'The application of this media in learning will have an impact on increasing the effectiveness, efficiency and attractiveness of learning Madura history and alphabet.'
engagement_results: The authors report that 'The students showed high enthusiasm for learning when they learned to use this Halo Madura educational game.' User trial scores (85-87%) suggest positive reception among students. The study notes the media can 'divert students to not only play other games that are entertainment in nature which has become a trend among children, especially elementary school students.'
comparative_methodology: No comparative methodology was used. The study employed a development research (R&D) approach using the ADDIE model. Evaluation consisted of expert validation (media design expert and material/content expert) and user testing at three scales (individual, small group, large group) using feasibility questionnaires with a 5-point scale: (1) Very low, (2) Less High, (3) High Enough, (4) High, (5) Very High.

title: When Everyone Wins: Dialogue, Play, and Black History for Critical Games Education
key_outcomes: Four of eight student-designed Harriet Tubman board games were selected for inclusion in a public exhibition at a local art gallery (The Albany Barn), representing a 50% 'success rate.' The authors note this reflects the pedagogical challenges of the course where some students struggled with connecting to the historical material. The four selected games (Guided, Combahee, Safehouse, Family or Foe?) demonstrated 'genuine engagement and curiosity to the story of Tubman' and teams 'were open to receiving constructive feedback on improving their designs.' Students who created successful games demonstrated critical media literacies including the ability to 'articulate the self as politically situated in mediatized culture' and 'communicate across differences.' The course produced powerful shifts: 'shifting focus from new to old, from white to black identity, from male to female identity, from simplification to complexity' in game design.
engagement_results: Mixed engagement results were observed. In successful dialogues, students demonstrated ability to listen and share 'across difference,' acknowledged 'their intersectional entanglement with games, society, and each other,' and displayed willingness to ask difficult questions. One student (Sarah, a Black female, two years later) reported: 'That intersection of history, social issues, and thought-provoking conversation, in my opinion, is greatly overlooked and underrepresented in the game industry at large.' Another student (Matthew, a white male, two years later) reported: 'it encouraged student engagement, resulting in us having to reflect and think more about the material taught instead of us just listening to the professor.' However, the study also documented significant resistance: some students dismissed dialogues, lacked engagement, and resisted learning through discomfort. In one dialogue, a white male student left the classroom for a quarter of an hour. Some students maintained that games are 'just for fun' and that culture is 'outside the purview of games.' The authors note that 'not all students were able to deeply engage the critical concepts we were asking them to reflect on.'
comparative_methodology: No comparative methodology was used. The study employs qualitative reflective analysis drawing on student dialogue transcripts, instructor observations, student game design artifacts, survey responses, and two longitudinal student reflections collected two years after the course. The authors explicitly note: 'As opposed to more instrumentalized forms of pedagogy, our assessment and outcomes are not focused on the evaluation of something our students produce as an end in itself (a research paper, a project, etc.). Instead, we are observing for evidence of deep connections within the group, between the students, and between students and the complexity of the subject.'

title: Work, Trade, Learn: Developing an Immersive Serious Game for History Education
statistical_results: Knowledge test (pre vs. post): Shapiro-Wilk W = 0.96, p = 0.16 (normal); paired samples t-test: post-test M = 3.39, SD = 1.27 significantly higher than pre-test M = 1.66, SD = 1.08; t(37) = 6.113, p < 0.001. Knowledge gain comparison between conditions: Desktop M = 1.95, SD = 1.28 vs. VR M = 1.53, SD = 1.76; independent samples t-test t(36) = 0.82, p = 0.42 (not significant). Levene test F = 2.95, p = 0.09. Knowledge after 2 weeks vs. pre-test: Shapiro-Wilk W = 0.91, p < 0.01 (non-normal); Wilcoxon signed rank test: 2-week M = 3.00, SD = 1.11 significantly higher than pre-test M = 1.74, SD = 1.09; Z = 6.5, p < 0.001. Knowledge after 2 weeks vs. post-test: Shapiro-Wilk W = 0.93, p < 0.05 (non-normal); Wilcoxon signed rank test: 2-week M = 3.00, SD = 1.11 not significantly different from post-test M = 3.32, SD = 1.30; Z = 217, p = 0.13. 2-week knowledge gain between conditions: Desktop M = 1.32, SD = 0.98 vs. VR M = 1.2, SD = 0.98; Mann-Whitney U = 149.5, p = 0.81 (not significant). Topic interest (pre vs. post): Shapiro-Wilk W = 0.96, p = 0.23 (normal); paired t-test: post-test M = 20.8, SD = 5.54 significantly higher than pre-test M = 19.58, SD = 6.03; t(37) = 2.58, p < 0.05. Topic interest gain between conditions: Desktop M = 1.47, SD = 2.66 vs. VR M = 1.05, SD = 3.25; independent samples t-test t(36) = 0.43, p = 0.67 (not significant). Situational interest comparison: Desktop M = 31.58, SD = 5.30 vs. VR M = 29.11, SD = 5.60; independent samples t-test t(36) = -0.88, p = 0.38 (not significant).
key_outcomes: The serious game significantly increased participants' knowledge of history from pre-test to post-test (p < 0.001), with scores roughly doubling from M = 1.66 to M = 3.39 out of 5. Knowledge gains persisted at the 2-week follow-up (M = 3.00, significantly higher than pre-test, p < 0.001) and were not significantly different from immediate post-test scores (p = 0.13), suggesting lasting retention. Topic interest in history also significantly increased after playing (p < 0.05). However, there was no significant difference between VR and Desktop conditions on any measure: knowledge gain, 2-week retention, topic interest change, or situational interest. Hypotheses H1, H3, and H6 were supported (knowledge increase, topic interest increase, 2-week retention). Hypotheses H2, H4, H5, and H7 were rejected (no VR advantage over Desktop on any measure).
engagement_results: Situational interest did not differ significantly between conditions (Desktop M = 31.58, SD = 5.30 vs. VR M = 29.11, SD = 5.60; t(36) = -0.88, p = 0.38). Qualitative positive feedback: 10 participants liked the controls, 8 each liked the tasks, virtual environment, and character dialogues, and 4 liked the object highlighting system. Qualitative negative feedback: 11 participants wanted better graphics, 5 wanted more interactive elements, 4 wanted more content, and 3 criticized the controls.
comparative_methodology: Between-subjects experimental design with two conditions: VR (immersive VR with HTC Vive HMD) and Desktop-3D (standard PC with keyboard/mouse). 19 participants per condition, randomly assigned. Pre-test and post-test knowledge assessments, with additional 2-week follow-up (34 of 38 completed). Knowledge gains compared between conditions using independent samples t-tests, Mann-Whitney U tests, or Wilcoxon signed rank tests depending on normality. Statistical analysis performed using R in R-Studio.

title: Your iPhone Cannot Escape History, and Neither Can You: Self-Reflexive Design for a Mobile History Learning Game
key_outcomes: The study reports qualitative outcomes across three design iterations of the self-reflexive element: (1) In the pilot iteration, only a few students completed the game and did not receive the Foxconn news story (the self-reflexive reveal). (2) In the first iteration, after adding an Afikoman (hidden bonus containing the contemporary articles), some students picked up the tip but did not read the article about Foxconn, jumping ahead to complete the game. One girl's short answer revealed lack of connection to enduring historical themes despite exposure. (3) In the final iteration, using a 'suprareveal' strategy (presenting a Bangladesh factory collapse article at the start of the game rather than only at the end), discussions of the factory collapse began immediately. There was 'no evidence in either postgame interviews or open-ended answers on postgame surveys of lack of awareness of the contemporary global issues of worker safety.' The suprareveal approach was found to offset 'issues of lack of attention to contemporary cases as well as provide a conscious frame for the game to come.'
engagement_results: Qualitative engagement observations: In the final iteration with the suprareveal, learners read the Bangladesh article out loud prior to the game and asked questions about the article, demonstrating evidence of awareness of the historic theme. Players asked questions like 'What does this article have to do with Jewish history?' and 'What is the date on the article?' indicating active engagement with the contemporary content. There was a shift from evidence of lack of awareness regarding contemporary labor struggles to an iteration 'devoid of disconfirming cases of awareness.' The Foxconn and Bangladesh articles, when used together, generated discussion of contemporary labor disputes in the context of historic labor disputes and eliminated confusion and erroneous conclusions about contemporary labor disputes.
comparative_methodology: Design-based research with iterative design cycles. Data collection included pre- and post-survey data, interviews, video and audio observation of players, and ARIS back-end server logs tracking each player's moves. Three design iterations were conducted across six game events, with analysis between iterations informing design modifications. No formal statistical comparisons are reported in this chapter; the author notes that full data sets and detailed description of the full study are published elsewhere (Gottlieb, 2015).
